items.title: WWI was triggered by a wrong turn
items.claim: On 28 June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand survived the first assassination attempt that morning. What caused the second, successful attempt hours later?

options.text: A coordinated second wave of assassins ambushed his motorcade on the way to the hospital
His driver took a wrong turn into a side street, stalled the car, and stopped directly in front of Gavrilo Princip
Princip followed the motorcade by tram and intercepted it at the town hall
A Serbian double agent inside the security detail signalled his location

items.reveal_title: A wrong turn into world war
items.reveal:
After a bomb attack that morning failed, the Archduke insisted on visiting the wounded at the hospital. His driver, Leopold Lojka, had not been told the route had been changed. He turned right onto Franz Joseph Street, was told he was going the wrong way, and stalled while reversing.

Gavrilo Princip, who had given up and was eating a sandwich (the sandwich story is disputed but he was at Schiller's delicatessen), happened to be standing there. He stepped forward and fired twice from five feet away.
items.why: The 'causes of WWI' essay tends to load every variable onto structural forces (alliances, militarism, imperialism). Those forces created the powder keg, but a stalled car lit the fuse. Contingency matters.

items.title: Hitler nearly walked out of the Nazi Party in 1921
items.claim: In July 1921, Hitler threatened to resign from the NSDAP unless he was given dictatorial control. What happened?

options.text: He was expelled and founded a rival party
The committee accepted his terms by a vote of 543 to 1 — the lone dissenter being a printer named Posch
He was forced to share leadership with Anton Drexler
The party split in two, with Hitler taking the Munich faction

items.reveal:
Anton Drexler had founded the German Workers' Party in 1919. Hitler joined in September 1919 as member 555 (the numbering started at 500 to inflate membership). By 1921 he was the party's most effective speaker.

When Drexler tried to merge with another nationalist group, Hitler resigned in protest, then demanded the chairmanship with dictatorial powers as the price of returning. The 29 July 1921 vote went 543 to 1.
items.why: Hitler's rise feels inevitable in hindsight. In 1921 he was a fringe agitator in a fringe party negotiating his way to control of an organisation with no national presence. Contingency, again.

items.title: Lenin tried to remove Stalin from his deathbed
items.claim: In late 1922 and early 1923, Lenin dictated a 'Testament' commenting on his potential successors. What did it say about Stalin?

options.text: It praised Stalin as the most capable administrator and probable successor
It called Stalin 'too rude' and proposed removing him from his post as General Secretary
It did not mention Stalin at all
It endorsed Stalin only as a temporary compromise with Trotsky

items.reveal_title: Suppressed by the man it condemned
items.reveal:
In a postscript dictated on 4 January 1923, Lenin wrote: 'Stalin is too rude and this defect... becomes intolerable in a Secretary-General. That is why I suggest that the comrades think about a way of removing Stalin from that post.'

After Lenin's death in January 1924, the Testament was read at the Central Committee but suppressed. Stalin offered to resign at the 13th Congress; the offer was rejected and the document was buried. It was not published in the USSR until 1956 under Khrushchev.
items.why: Stalin's consolidation of power was not authorised by Lenin — it was achieved despite Lenin's explicit, dying objection. The myth of Stalin as Lenin's chosen heir was built later.

items.title: Roman concrete is stronger now than when it was poured
items.claim: Modern concrete piers in seawater typically last 50-100 years. The Roman harbour at Caesarea Maritima, built around 22 BC, is still standing. Why?

options.text: The Romans used a deeper foundation technique that modern engineers have abandoned
Seawater reacts with volcanic ash in the mix to grow aluminous tobermorite crystals that strengthen the concrete over centuries
Roman concrete contained iron filaments that prevented cracking
The Mediterranean's low salinity preserves concrete better than the open ocean

items.reveal:
MIT and Berkeley researchers (Marie Jackson and colleagues, published 2017) analysed cores from Roman marine structures. The Roman mix used pozzolana — volcanic ash from the Bay of Naples — combined with lime and seawater.

When seawater percolates through cracks, it reacts with the ash to precipitate aluminous tobermorite and phillipsite crystals that fill the cracks. The concrete literally heals and strengthens over time.
items.why: Progress narratives assume modern technology is always superior. Roman marine concrete is a case where ancient empirical knowledge produced a material modern engineering struggles to match.

items.title: Napoleon was average height — possibly slightly above
items.claim: Napoleon's autopsy in 1821 recorded his height. What was it, by modern measurement?

options.text: 5 ft 2 in (157 cm) — short even for his time
5 ft 7 in (169-170 cm) — average to slightly above average for a Frenchman of his generation
5 ft 10 in (178 cm) — unusually tall for his time
There is no reliable record of his height

items.reveal:
The autopsy recorded Napoleon at 5 feet 2 inches — in French pre-metric units (pied du roi). A French inch was longer than an English inch. Converted, that's roughly 5 feet 6.5 to 5 feet 7 inches (169-170 cm).

The average French male conscript of the period was around 164 cm. British caricaturists, especially James Gillray, popularised the short-Napoleon trope as propaganda. He was also usually surrounded by his Imperial Guard, who were selected for height.
items.why: A historical 'fact' everyone knows can be a unit-conversion error amplified by propaganda. Always check the source — and the units.

items.title: Medieval Europeans knew the Earth was round
items.claim: The idea that 'medieval people thought the Earth was flat' was popularised in the 19th century. Who is most responsible for spreading it?

options.text: Galileo, in his trial defence of 1633
Christopher Columbus's biographers in the 1490s
Washington Irving's 1828 biography of Columbus, which fabricated a debate at Salamanca about whether Columbus would sail off the edge
Karl Marx, as part of his critique of religion

items.reveal:
Bede (8th century), Aquinas (13th century), Dante (14th century) and the entire scholastic tradition assumed a spherical Earth — it was Aristotelian orthodoxy reinforced by Ptolemy. Columbus's argument with the Salamanca scholars was about the Earth's circumference, not its shape; they thought (correctly) it was too large to sail to Asia westward.

Washington Irving's 'A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus' (1828) was a partly fictionalised popular biography. It invented the flat-Earth debate to make Columbus look more visionary. The myth then became a stock anti-medieval, anti-Catholic talking point in the late 19th century (notably John William Draper and Andrew Dickson White).
items.why: Historiography matters. The 'Dark Ages' frame and the flat-Earth myth are products of later polemic, not medieval thought. The conflict-between-science-and-religion narrative is largely a 19th-century construction.

items.title: One Soviet officer's veto prevented nuclear war in 1962
items.claim: On 27 October 1962, a Soviet submarine (B-59) near Cuba was being depth-charged by the US Navy. The captain ordered a nuclear torpedo prepared for launch. Why didn't it fire?

options.text: The torpedo malfunctioned
Launch required the unanimous consent of three officers; Second Captain Vasily Arkhipov refused
Kennedy's blockade orders explicitly forbade depth-charging Soviet submarines
The submarine surfaced before the launch could be authorised

items.reveal_title: The man who saved the world
items.reveal:
B-59 had been submerged for days, the air was foul, the crew thought war had begun. Captain Valentin Savitsky and political officer Ivan Maslennikov voted to fire. Arkhipov, brigade chief of staff and equal in rank, refused.

Under Soviet protocol, all three had to agree. Arkhipov persuaded Savitsky to surface and await orders. The story only emerged publicly in 2002 at a conference marking the crisis's 40th anniversary; Thomas Blanton of the National Security Archive said 'a guy called Vasily Arkhipov saved the world.'
items.why: Macro-historical narratives about MAD (mutually assured destruction) keeping the peace miss that systems are only as safe as the individuals inside them. Nuclear war was a vote away.

items.title: Rosa Parks was a trained activist, not a tired seamstress
items.claim: Rosa Parks's December 1955 refusal to give up her bus seat is often told as a spontaneous act. What was her actual background?

options.text: She had no prior political involvement and acted purely on impulse
She was secretary of the Montgomery NAACP and had attended training at the Highlander Folk School months earlier
She was a paid organiser sent specifically to provoke an arrest
She was a member of the Communist Party, which is why she was arrested

items.reveal:
Parks had been Montgomery NAACP secretary since 1943. In summer 1955 she attended a workshop at Highlander Folk School in Tennessee on desegregation strategy. She was also not the first to refuse — Claudette Colvin had done the same in March 1955 but was 15, pregnant, and considered unsuitable as a test case by the NAACP.

Parks later wrote: 'People always say that I didn't give up my seat because I was tired, but that isn't true... the only tired I was, was tired of giving in.'
items.why: The 'tired seamstress' story makes civil rights feel like an accident of individual virtue. The actual story is one of organised, strategic activism — which is harder to teach but truer.

items.title: Harold won the first battle of 1066 — then lost the second three weeks later
items.claim: King Harold Godwinson fought two major battles in 1066. What happened?

options.text: Hastings was his only battle of the year
He defeated Harald Hardrada and Tostig at Stamford Bridge on 25 September, then marched 250 miles south and lost to William at Hastings on 14 October
He won at Hastings but died of wounds soon after
He defeated William at Hastings, then was killed by Harald Hardrada

items.reveal:
Harald Hardrada of Norway and Harold's exiled brother Tostig landed in Yorkshire in September 1066. Harold marched north and crushed them at Stamford Bridge on 25 September — Hardrada and Tostig were killed.

Three days later William of Normandy landed at Pevensey. Harold's exhausted army marched south and met William at Senlac Hill near Hastings on 14 October. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records Harold's death; the Bayeux Tapestry depicts a figure with an arrow to the eye, though the identification is debated.
items.why: The Conquest is taught as a single event. It was actually a year of crisis with two invasions, one of which Harold won. Without Stamford Bridge weakening his army, Hastings might have gone the other way.

items.title: The Domesday Book recorded almost every pig in England
items.claim: William I commissioned the Domesday survey in 1085, completed 1086. How detailed was it?

options.text: It listed only the major landholders and royal manors
It recorded landholders, ploughs, mills, fishponds, livestock and even individual peasants down to the level of swineherds — over 13,000 places
It was a list of military obligations only
It covered only southern England

items.reveal_title: Not one ox or cow escaped
items.reveal:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (E text) complained: 'So very narrowly did he have it investigated that there was no single hide nor a yard of land, nor indeed (it is a shame to relate but it seemed no shame to him to do) one ox nor one cow nor one pig which was left out.'

Commissioners visited every shire, took sworn testimony, and produced the survey in around a year. The original manuscripts (Great Domesday and Little Domesday) survive at The National Archives, Kew.
items.why: Medieval government is often dismissed as primitive. Domesday is more administratively detailed than anything attempted in Europe for centuries afterwards.

items.title: Magna Carta was annulled within ten weeks
items.claim: King John sealed Magna Carta at Runnymede on 15 June 1215. What happened next?

options.text: It immediately became the basis of English liberty and was respected by the crown
John wrote to Pope Innocent III, who annulled it as 'shameful and demeaning' on 24 August 1215 — civil war resumed
John was forced to confirm it in Parliament the following year
It was burned by the barons after John refused to enforce it

items.reveal:
Pope Innocent III's bull of 24 August 1215 declared Magna Carta 'null and void of all validity forever', calling it extorted by force. The First Barons' War followed; the barons invited Prince Louis of France to take the throne.

John died of dysentery in October 1216. The charter was reissued by the regents of his nine-year-old son Henry III to win support — that is the version that took root. The 1297 reissue under Edward I is the one on the statute roll.
items.why: Magna Carta as 'the foundation of liberty' is a 17th-century invention (Coke). In 1215 it was a peace treaty between a desperate king and rebellious barons — and it failed within weeks.

items.title: The Black Death killed perhaps half of Europe
items.claim: The plague reached England in 1348. What proportion of the European population died in the first wave (1346-1353)?

options.text: About 5-10%
Roughly 30-60% — estimates centre around 40-50% of Europe's population
Less than 20% in most regions
Around 75% of the urban population only

items.reveal:
Ole Benedictow's revised estimates (2021) put European mortality at around 60%. Earlier consensus was a third to a half. Either way it is the largest mortality event in European history.

The plague returned roughly every generation until the 17th century. Wages rose, labour shortages broke serfdom, and the Statute of Labourers (1351) tried — and failed — to peg wages back. The 1381 Peasants' Revolt is one downstream consequence.
items.why: Numbers matter. A 5% pandemic is a crisis; a 50% pandemic is a different kind of event — it reshapes economy, religion and demography for centuries.

items.title: The 14-year-old Richard II rode out to meet the rebels at Smithfield
items.claim: On 15 June 1381 the Peasants' Revolt ended at Smithfield. What actually happened?

options.text: The king's army defeated the rebels in open battle
Wat Tyler was killed by William Walworth, mayor of London, and Richard II rode forward and persuaded the crowd he would be their new leader
The rebels stormed the Tower of London and forced Richard to abdicate
John of Gaunt negotiated a settlement that gave rebels permanent rights

items.reveal_title: A teenage king and a dead leader
items.reveal:
Walworth stabbed Tyler during a parley. As Tyler fell, Richard II — aged 14 — rode forward and said 'You shall have no captain but me'. The rebels dispersed.

The charters Richard granted were revoked within weeks. John Ball was hanged, drawn and quartered in July. Richard reportedly told a later petition: 'Villeins ye are, and villeins ye shall remain.' The poll tax was nonetheless quietly dropped.
items.why: Successful revolts are rare and brief. The 1381 rising failed in its immediate aims but ended the experiment with poll taxes for 600 years — until 1990.

items.title: The Hundred Years War lasted 116 years
items.claim: When did the Hundred Years War begin and end?

options.text: 1300-1400, exactly a century
1337 (Edward III claims the French throne) to 1453 (Battle of Castillon) — 116 years, with long truces in between
1346-1446, from Crecy to the end
1415-1515, from Agincourt onwards

items.reveal_title: A name invented in the 19th century
items.reveal:
The phrase 'Hundred Years War' was coined by French historians in the 1860s. Contemporaries did not see it as a single conflict but as a series of campaigns separated by long peaces (e.g. the Treaty of Brétigny, 1360).

Major English victories: Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356), Agincourt (1415). Major French recoveries: Du Guesclin's reconquests under Charles V, and Joan of Arc's relief of Orléans (1429). It ended with the French victory at Castillon in 1453 — three months before Constantinople fell.
items.why: Periodisation is a historical choice, not a fact. A '100 years' war that was actually 116, mostly truce, and named four centuries later is a useful reminder.

items.title: Nobody called it the Wars of the Roses at the time
items.claim: The wars between Lancaster and York (1455-1487) are remembered for the red and white rose badges. What is the actual history of those symbols?

options.text: Both sides wore rose badges throughout the conflict
The white rose was a Yorkist badge, but the red Lancastrian rose was largely a Tudor-era invention — Henry VII used the union of the roses as propaganda
The roses came from heraldic tradition dating to the Conquest
The name was coined in 1485 by Henry VII himself

items.reveal_title: The Tudor rose was the spin
items.reveal:
Edward IV used a white rose among other badges. The red rose was a minor Lancastrian badge under Henry IV but rarely used during the wars themselves. The 'Tudor rose' (red and white combined) was created after Henry VII married Elizabeth of York in 1486 — the union as legitimising symbol.

The name 'Wars of the Roses' was popularised by Walter Scott's novel 'Anne of Geierstein' (1829). Shakespeare's 'Henry VI Part 1' invented the Temple Garden scene where nobles pluck the rival roses.
items.why: Historical memory is shaped by later spin. The Tudor regime had every reason to dramatise dynastic union; Shakespeare amplified the imagery; Scott named it. Almost none of that was visible in 1460.

items.title: Henry VII was a 'modern' monarch — by destroying the nobility
items.claim: How did Henry VII (r. 1485-1509) consolidate power?

options.text: By distributing land widely among loyal nobles
By using bonds and recognisances to financially bind nobles, the Star Chamber to bypass juries, and avoiding war to keep crown finances strong
By creating a standing army of 50,000 men
By moving the capital from London to York

items.reveal:
Henry VII forced nobles to enter bonds — written debts payable to the crown on bad behaviour. By 1509 around two-thirds of the peerage was under bond. Empson and Dudley managed crown revenue ruthlessly.

The Star Chamber, sitting at Westminster, dealt with cases the common-law courts could not — overmighty nobles intimidating juries. Henry VII left £1.5 million in the treasury (his son spent it in a decade). He fought one continental war.
items.why: Henry VII is the boring Tudor — but his fiscal-administrative state is what makes Henry VIII's ambition possible. Modern bureaucratic monarchy starts here, not at the Reformation.

items.title: The Dissolution of the Monasteries was a wealth transfer
items.claim: Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries (1536-1541). How much was at stake financially?

options.text: A symbolic amount; most monasteries were poor
The monasteries owned around a quarter of the cultivated land in England; their dissolution transferred wealth equivalent to several times the crown's annual income
The proceeds were used to found grammar schools across the country
Only the buildings were seized; lands remained in religious hands

items.reveal:
Thomas Cromwell's Valor Ecclesiasticus (1535) surveyed monastic incomes — around £160,000 a year, against royal ordinary revenue of about £100,000. The Court of Augmentations was created to handle the proceeds.

Much of the land was sold below market to gentry buyers, creating a new class with a stake in keeping the Reformation. Cathedrals like Glastonbury were destroyed; libraries were dispersed (John Leland's lament). The wealth was largely spent on war with France within a decade.
items.why: The break with Rome was about Anne Boleyn and the king's conscience — but it was also the biggest fiscal opportunity an English king had had since the Conquest. Mixed motives, both real.

items.title: Henry VIII didn't divorce his first wife — he had the marriage annulled
items.claim: Henry VIII's first marriage ended in 1533. What is the technically correct description?

options.text: A divorce granted by Parliament
An annulment — Archbishop Cranmer declared the marriage to Catherine of Aragon had never been valid
A separation only, with Catherine retaining queenly status
A papal divorce granted by Clement VII

items.reveal:
Henry argued that his marriage to Catherine — his brother Arthur's widow — was barred by Leviticus 20:21. Cranmer's court at Dunstable in May 1533 declared the marriage void from the start.

The distinction matters: annulment says no marriage existed; divorce ends a valid one. Mary I's legitimacy depended on which view prevailed (the Second Act of Succession, 1536, made her illegitimate; the Third, 1543, restored her in line). Catherine refused to accept the annulment until her death in 1536.
items.why: The vocabulary of Tudor religion is technical. 'Divorce' makes it sound modern; 'annulment' shows it as a legal claim about the past — which is why the marriage to Anne could be valid at all.

items.title: Elizabeth I owned around 80 wigs and 2,000 dresses
items.claim: Elizabeth I's image — the painted face, the wigs — was carefully constructed. How extensive was the wardrobe?

options.text: A handful of ceremonial robes for state occasions only
Inventories at her death (1603) recorded around 2,000 gowns and roughly 80 wigs, with ceruse make-up to mask smallpox scarring from 1562
She refused jewels and dressed plainly throughout her reign
She owned 7,000 wigs alone

items.reveal:
Elizabeth survived smallpox in October 1562 with scarring on her face and neck. She used ceruse (white lead and vinegar) to whiten her skin — slowly poisonous.

Nicholas Hilliard's 'Treatise Concerning the Arte of Limning' notes that after about 1590 painters were instructed not to show shadow on her face — the 'Mask of Youth' image. The wardrobe was a political instrument: gifts from courtiers carried specific meanings.
items.why: Elizabeth's reign was a sustained exercise in image management. The 'Gloriana' iconography was deliberate state branding, not personal vanity.

items.title: The English Reformation was not popular
items.claim: What did Eamon Duffy's 'The Stripping of the Altars' (1992) argue?

options.text: That the English laity were already Protestant in spirit before 1530 and welcomed the changes
That late medieval Catholicism was vigorous and popular, and the Reformation was imposed from above against widespread reluctance
That the Reformation made no real impact below the level of the elite
That the Pilgrimage of Grace (1536) succeeded in halting reform

items.reveal:
Duffy used churchwardens' accounts, wills and surviving objects to argue that late medieval English Catholic devotion was rich, complex and widely engaged — not a corrupt system waiting to be reformed.

The Pilgrimage of Grace (1536) involved perhaps 40,000 northern rebels protesting against the dissolution. The 1549 Western Rising opposed the new Prayer Book. Mary I's restoration of Catholicism (1553-1558) was popular in much of the country.

A. G. Dickens's older 'English Reformation' (1964) had emphasised popular Protestant momentum; Duffy reversed that picture.
items.why: Whether a change was 'demanded from below' or 'imposed from above' is a structural question about how change works. Both can be true at once, but the balance matters for how we read the period.

items.title: Mary I burned around 280 Protestants
items.claim: Mary I's reign (1553-1558) earned the 'Bloody Mary' epithet through executions. How many died?

options.text: Around 10,000 — comparable to Henry VIII's executions
Around 280 Protestants burned at the stake, plus 30 who died in prison — a smaller toll than Henry VIII's or Elizabeth I's overall execution numbers
Over 50,000 in a state campaign of terror
No confirmed executions for religion — the epithet is entirely myth

items.reveal:
John Foxe's 'Actes and Monuments' (1563, later 'Foxe's Book of Martyrs') chronicled the Marian burnings in vivid detail and became a foundational Protestant text. Henry VIII executed an estimated 57,000 (Holinshed's figure, contested) including thousands of vagrants; Elizabeth I executed around 200 Catholic priests and Jesuits.

Mary's numbers were lower in absolute terms but concentrated (1555-1558) and ideological. The propaganda effect outlasted the regime.
items.why: Reputation is unevenly distributed. Mary's image as uniquely cruel says more about the durability of Protestant propaganda than about Tudor execution rates.

items.title: Charles I lost the Civil War partly because he was a poor commander
items.claim: What contributed to Charles I's defeat (1642-1646) beyond political 'tyranny'?

options.text: Parliamentary forces always vastly outnumbered the king's

Parliament held London (wealth, manpower), the navy, and after 1645 the New Model Army; Charles repeatedly failed to coordinate his commanders and missed strategic opportunities like marching on London after Edgehill
The Scots refused to fight on either side
Charles was killed in battle at Naseby

items.reveal_title: The man, not just the cause
items.reveal:
After the indecisive Edgehill (October 1642), Charles failed to march on London while it was undefended. The Solemn League and Covenant (1643) brought Scottish forces in on Parliament's side. The New Model Army (formed 1645) under Fairfax and Cromwell was the first national professional army.

Charles surrendered to the Scots in 1646; they handed him to Parliament. His attempts to negotiate while plotting a second war (the 'Engagement' with the Scots, 1647) destroyed any remaining trust and led to his trial.
items.why: Wars are won by armies, logistics and leadership — not just by who has the better political argument. Charles's strategic failures are often glossed over in the rush to debate 'tyranny vs liberty'.

items.title: Cromwell did not set out to be a republican
items.claim: What were Oliver Cromwell's politics in 1642?

options.text: He had been a republican agitator since the 1620s
He was a Huntingdonshire MP and country gentleman who fought for Parliament against the king's policies but moved towards regicide only by late 1648
He was a paid Dutch agent from the start
He was a Leveller from the outset

items.reveal:
Cromwell entered the 1640 Long Parliament as MP for Cambridge. As late as 1647 he was negotiating with Charles I (the Heads of the Proposals). The king's plotting with the Scots — the Second Civil War of 1648 — convinced Cromwell that Charles could not be trusted.

Pride's Purge (December 1648) removed MPs likely to negotiate. The Rump Parliament tried and executed the king on 30 January 1649. Cromwell signed the death warrant but had not been pushing for it years earlier.

He later dissolved the Rump (1653) and accepted the title Lord Protector, refusing the crown in 1657.
items.why: The 'inevitable republican' Cromwell of memory is partly constructed by 19th-century liberals (Macaulay, Carlyle). The actual man's politics shifted under pressure of events.

items.title: The Glorious Revolution was a Dutch invasion
items.claim: William of Orange landed in Devon on 5 November 1688. How large was the force?

options.text: A diplomatic mission of a few hundred men
Around 15,000 troops on 463 ships — larger than the Spanish Armada
Only James II's English defectors, no foreign troops
A small English army recruited in advance by Parliament

items.reveal:
Seven English nobles (the 'Immortal Seven') invited William in June 1688. He landed at Brixham, Devon, with 15,000-21,000 Dutch troops, plus thousands of horses and 50 cannon. James II's army melted; key officers (including John Churchill, the future Duke of Marlborough) defected.

James fled to France in December. The Convention Parliament (January 1689) declared the throne vacant and offered it to William and Mary. The Bill of Rights followed in December 1689.

The Williamite War in Ireland (Boyne 1690) and the Highland war in Scotland (Killiecrankie 1689) were anything but bloodless.
items.why: The 'Glorious Revolution' as bloodless English self-determination is a Whig myth. It was a foreign-backed coup with extensive bloodshed in Ireland and Scotland — successful, but not peaceful.

items.title: The Great Fire of London killed officially six people
items.claim: The Great Fire (2-6 September 1666) destroyed much of the medieval City. Official deaths?

options.text: Around 100,000 — comparable to the plague
Six officially recorded — though modern historians suspect more, especially among the poor
Around 10,000 in the City alone
No reliable count exists

items.reveal:
The fire destroyed 13,200 houses, 87 parish churches and St Paul's Cathedral over four days. It started at Thomas Farriner's bakery on Pudding Lane around 1 a.m. on 2 September. Samuel Pepys's diary is the most vivid account.

Only six deaths were officially recorded. Neil Hanson and others have argued the true toll was higher — the fire reached temperatures over 1,700 C, hot enough to vaporise human remains, and many of the poor were not formally counted.

The Great Plague of 1665 had killed around 100,000 — perhaps a quarter of London's population — the previous year.
items.why: Official numbers are not the whole story, but they're also not nothing. The plague (100,000) and the fire (six) sit oddly together in memory, but both shaped Restoration London.

items.title: The Luddites were skilled workers protecting trade standards
items.claim: Who were the Luddites (1811-1812)?

options.text: Anti-technology mystics who rejected all machinery
Skilled textile workers — stocking knitters, croppers, weavers — who smashed specific machines being used to produce low-quality goods by unapprenticed labour, often after pay cuts and food shortages
Foreign agitators paid by Napoleon
A peasants' revolt against enclosure

items.reveal:
The Luddites took their name from the mythical Ned Ludd. Their grievances were specific: wide stocking frames produced cut-up goods sold as stockings; gig-mills and shearing frames replaced cropping; manufacturers were ignoring the Statute of Artificers (1563) requiring seven-year apprenticeships.

The Frame-Breaking Act (1812) made machine-breaking a capital offence — Byron made his maiden speech in the Lords opposing it. 17 Luddites were hanged at York in January 1813. The historian E. P. Thompson's 'The Making of the English Working Class' (1963) rehabilitated them as political actors.
items.why: 'Luddite' as an insult against anyone who dislikes new technology obscures the actual movement. They were skilled tradesmen defending wages and standards against unregulated mechanisation — not opponents of machinery in principle.

items.title: Children under 10 worked underground in British coal mines until 1842
items.claim: What did the Mines Act of 1842 prohibit?

options.text: All child labour in the UK
Underground employment for women and girls, and for boys under 10 — following Lord Ashley's (later Shaftesbury) commission report with illustrations of children pulling coal trucks
Only women's underground work
Coal mining itself, switching the country to oil

items.reveal:
The 1842 Royal Commission report on children in mines included engravings of half-naked children — boys as young as 5 acting as 'trappers' opening ventilation doors, girls and women hauling coal in chains. The illustrations shocked Parliament.

The Act banned women and girls underground entirely and boys under 10. Earlier factory legislation (1819, 1833, 1844) limited child working hours and required schooling. Robert Owen's New Lanark mills (from 1800) had already shown a different model.
items.why: 'Reform' was driven partly by humanitarian shock and partly by middle-class anxiety about working-class women. The Acts solved one problem (underground child labour) without addressing others (above-ground work continued for decades).

items.title: Britain ran on local solar time until the railways forced standardisation
items.claim: When did Britain adopt a single national time?

options.text: After the 1707 Acts of Union
Railway companies adopted Greenwich Mean Time from 1840 (Great Western) to coordinate timetables; legal national time followed by the Definition of Time Act 1880
After WWI
Not until the 1950s when broadcasting required it

items.reveal:
Before railways, towns kept local solar time — Bristol was about 10 minutes behind London by the sun. Railway timetables made this unworkable. The Great Western Railway adopted GMT in 1840; most railways followed by 1848.

Local authorities resisted; the Exchange Clock at Bristol famously had two minute hands. The Definition of Time Act 1880 standardised legal time. The International Meridian Conference (Washington, 1884) set Greenwich as the prime meridian for the world.
items.why: The 'natural' experience of time is local. Industrial systems forced its standardisation — the railway is one of the first technologies to remake the perception of time itself.

items.title: Cholera transmission was solved by removing a pump handle
items.claim: In the 1854 Soho outbreak, what did John Snow do?

options.text: He developed the first cholera vaccine
He mapped deaths around Broad Street, identified the public water pump as the source, and persuaded authorities to remove its handle on 8 September 1854
He proved cholera was airborne
He invented chlorination of water

items.reveal:
Snow's spot map of Broad Street showed deaths clustered around one pump. He overruled the dominant 'miasma' (bad air) theory of disease.

The pump handle was removed and cases fell. The cause was a leaking cesspit contaminating the well. Snow published 'On the Mode of Communication of Cholera' in 1855 — but his germ theory was not widely accepted until the 1860s with Pasteur and Koch.

London's main response was Joseph Bazalgette's sewer system (1859-1875), built largely after the 'Great Stink' of 1858 made Parliament unbearable.
items.why: Public health is often credited to grand theories. The 1854 case shows that careful observation and a map could outperform the dominant medical theory of the day — even before the underlying biology was understood.

items.title: Most Roman emperors died violently
items.claim: Of the 69 Roman emperors from Augustus (27 BCE) to Theodosius I (395 CE), how many died of natural causes?

options.text: Almost all — emperors were generally well-protected
Roughly a third — the rest died by assassination, in battle, by suicide or under suspicious circumstances
All emperors after Nero were murdered
Around half died of plague

items.reveal:
Joseph Saleh and colleagues (2019) modelled imperial deaths and found violent end rates above 50% for the first 25 years of any reign. The Crisis of the Third Century (235-284) saw around 50 emperors and usurpers in 50 years.

Named assassinations: Caligula (41), Claudius (54, probably poisoned by Agrippina), Domitian (96), Commodus (192), Caracalla (217), Elagabalus (222) and many more. Some died in war (Decius at Abrittus, 251; Valerian captured by the Persians, 260).
items.why: The imperial succession looks orderly from the list of names. Statistically, becoming emperor was one of the most dangerous jobs in the ancient world — which itself shaped imperial policy.

items.title: Eratosthenes calculated Earth's circumference within 1-15%
items.claim: Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes of Cyrene calculated Earth's circumference using shadows. How accurate was he?

options.text: Off by an order of magnitude
His value (around 250,000 stadia) is, depending on which stadion he used, within 1-15% of the modern value of ~40,075 km
His method was sound but he had no actual figure
He was the first to argue Earth was flat

items.reveal_title: Two sticks and a hired pacer
items.reveal:
Eratosthenes knew the sun shone straight down a well at Syene (Aswan) at noon on the summer solstice. At Alexandria, a vertical stick cast a shadow at the same moment, with an angle of about 1/50 of a circle (7.2°). He paid a 'bematist' (professional pacer) to measure the distance — about 5,000 stadia.

50 × 5,000 = 250,000 stadia. The exact length of a stadion is uncertain (157 m to 185 m), giving a circumference between ~39,000 km and ~46,000 km. The true value is 40,075 km at the equator.
items.why: The 'ancients thought Earth was flat' myth is wrong about both the ancients and the science. Greek geometry was capable of measuring planetary dimensions to within a few percent over 2,200 years ago.

items.title: The Pyramids were built by paid workers, not slaves
items.claim: Who built the Great Pyramid at Giza (c. 2560 BCE)?

options.text: Hebrew slaves from Egypt
Skilled Egyptian craftsmen and rotating teams of agricultural workers, housed in a workers' town with bakeries and medical care — graves of those who died on the job have been found
Forced labour from Egypt's foreign conquests only
Mercenaries paid in gold from Nubia

items.reveal_title: A workforce, not a chain gang
items.reveal:
Mark Lehner and Zahi Hawass excavated the workers' town south of the Giza plateau from the 1980s. They found bakeries producing thousands of loaves daily, fish-processing areas, a medical facility and graves with healed injuries — evidence of long-term care.

Graffiti in the relieving chambers of the Great Pyramid records work-gang names ('Friends of Khufu', 'Drunkards of Menkaure'). Estimates suggest a permanent workforce of perhaps 4,000-5,000 with seasonal labour bringing it to 20,000.

The slave-building myth comes partly from Herodotus (5th century BCE, writing 2,000 years later) and partly from biblical-cinema conflation with the Exodus story.
items.why: The Pyramids as monuments to oppression is a cultural cliché. The archaeological record shows organised state labour with bread rations and beer — not chained slaves under whips.

items.title: Sumerian workers were paid in beer
items.claim: What did Sumerian wage records typically include?

options.text: Silver coins only
Rations of barley, oil, wool and beer — temple and palace workers received daily beer allowances, with the 'sila' as a standard measure
Grain alone with no fermented products
Slaves only; free workers were not paid

items.reveal_title: From the world's oldest pay slips
items.reveal:
Sumerian administrative tablets from Ur, Lagash and Umma (c. 3000-2000 BCE) record beer rations of around 1-5 sila (~1-5 litres) per day for workers. The Hymn to Ninkasi (c. 1800 BCE) is a recipe-prayer to the beer goddess.

Beer was safer than river water and a major calorie source. The Alulu beer receipt (c. 2050 BCE) is one of the oldest known commercial documents. Coinage was not invented until around the 7th century BCE in Lydia.
items.why: Money is a recent invention. Most ancient economies ran on rations, barter and grain-equivalents. The image of a wage economy with coinage is medieval and modern, not ancient.

items.title: Tutankhamun was minor — fame comes from an intact tomb
items.claim: Why is Tutankhamun (r. c. 1332-1323 BCE) so famous?

options.text: He was the greatest of all New Kingdom pharaohs
He was a young, minor pharaoh whose tomb (KV62) was found nearly intact by Howard Carter on 4 November 1922 — almost the only royal tomb to escape ancient looting
He led the Egyptians to defeat the Hittites
He was the first pharaoh to build a pyramid

items.reveal:
Tutankhamun died around age 19 after a reign of about 9 years. He partially reversed his father Akhenaten's religious reforms but his reign was historically minor.

Carter, funded by Lord Carnarvon, found a single step on 4 November 1922 after years of fruitless digging. On 26 November he made a small hole, held up a candle, and when asked if he could see anything famously replied 'Yes, wonderful things'. The tomb contained over 5,000 artefacts. Carnarvon died of an infected mosquito bite in April 1923, fuelling 'curse' stories.
items.why: Fame is not the same as historical importance. Tutankhamun's celebrity is an artefact of preservation and 20th-century media, not of what he actually did.

items.title: Anglo-Saxon law replaced revenge with a price list
items.claim: What was 'wergild'?

options.text: A trial by combat for serious crimes
A 'man-price' — compensation paid to a victim's family or to a victim of injury, set by social rank (a king's wergild far higher than a ceorl's) to end blood feuds
A village court system
A property tax owed to the lord

items.reveal:
Aethelberht's law code (Kent, c. 600 CE) — the earliest surviving English legal text — sets compensation for injuries with itemised precision: four shillings for an outer ear, twelve for the inner. Murder of a freeman (ceorl) was 200 shillings; a thegn 600; a king's son much higher.

Wergild aimed to substitute payment for cyclical feud. It coexisted with the death penalty for some offences (theft, treason). The Norman Conquest gradually replaced wergild with crown justice — crimes against the king's peace rather than against persons.
items.why: 'Justice' has had many shapes. Anglo-Saxon law was rational, written and surprisingly modern in seeing crime as economic harm — but built around social hierarchy in a way modern law explicitly rejects.

items.title: Georgian England had 200+ capital offences
items.claim: What was the 'Bloody Code' (c. 1688-1820s)?

options.text: A modernised criminal code that abolished hanging
The expansion of capital crimes from around 50 in 1688 to over 220 by 1815 — including stealing goods worth 12 pence from a shop
A medieval system of trial by ordeal
The system of cattle thieves' execution in Scotland only

items.reveal:
The Waltham Black Act (1723) alone created around 50 new capital offences. Many capital sentences were commuted (juries undervalued goods to avoid death penalty — 'pious perjury'), or replaced by transportation to America (until 1776) and Australia (from 1787).

Reformers — Samuel Romilly, Robert Peel as Home Secretary — gradually reduced the list. By 1841 only treason, murder and a handful of others remained capital. Public hangings at Tyburn ended in 1783 (moved to Newgate); the last public hanging was 1868.
items.why: The Bloody Code shows the early modern state using execution as a substitute for an effective police force. The Victorian shift to imprisonment + policing changes the whole structure of criminal justice.

items.title: London had no professional police force until 1829
items.claim: Who founded the Metropolitan Police and on what principles?

options.text: Henry Fielding, in 1750 (Bow Street Runners)
Home Secretary Robert Peel, Metropolitan Police Act 1829, with the principle that police derive authority from public consent — Peel's 'nine principles'
Queen Victoria personally in 1837
The Duke of Wellington as PM, modelled on military regiments

items.reveal:
The Met began with around 1,000 officers based at Scotland Yard. Uniforms were deliberately civilian-looking (blue, not the military red) to distinguish them from soldiers. Officers carried truncheons, not firearms.

The Fielding brothers' Bow Street Runners (1750) had been a small detective force. Peel's innovation was preventive uniformed patrol, full-time and salaried. Within decades every English borough had a force; the County Police Acts of 1839 and 1856 extended it nationwide.

Peel's nine principles — including 'the police are the public and the public are the police' — are still cited.
items.why: Modern policing is younger than the Industrial Revolution. The concept of a professional, preventive, public force is an early 19th-century invention with specific design choices that still shape British policing.

items.title: Around 50,000 Huguenots fled to England in the 1680s
items.claim: Why did French Huguenots come to England?

options.text: They were invited as agricultural labour by William III
Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes (1598) in 1685, removing Protestant rights — around 50,000 fled to England, with major settlements in Spitalfields, Soho and Canterbury
They were exiled by James II for Jacobite sympathies
Famine in Brittany drove migration in the 1680s

items.reveal:
The Revocation of the Edict of Nantes (October 1685) made Protestant worship illegal in France. Perhaps 200,000-400,000 Huguenots fled total — to England, the Dutch Republic, Brandenburg, the Cape and the American colonies.

In England they brought silk-weaving (Spitalfields), gunmaking, watchmaking, banking (the Courtauld and Bosanquet families). 'Refugee' as an English word enters the language from the Huguenot experience.

Charles II had already extended denizenship to French Protestants in 1681. Anti-Catholic sentiment made absorption relatively smooth.
items.why: Migration history in Britain is much older than the 20th century. The Huguenot case is the classic example of refugees whose skills shaped an industrial sector — and whose absorption was made easier by religious alignment.

items.title: The Windrush passengers were British subjects, not foreign immigrants
items.claim: On 22 June 1948 the HMT Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury with 492 passengers from the Caribbean. Their legal status?

options.text: They required visas and work permits
They were British subjects with full right of entry — the British Nationality Act 1948 confirmed Commonwealth citizens' status, passed weeks after Windrush
They were refugees with temporary leave
They were on military service tickets only

items.reveal:
The British Nationality Act 1948 (royal assent 30 July 1948) defined 'Citizens of the United Kingdom and Colonies' alongside Commonwealth citizenship. Caribbean people were British subjects; the journey required no permit.

The 1971 Immigration Act removed automatic right of abode for most Commonwealth citizens. People who had arrived as children before 1973 should have had right to remain, but the Home Office destroyed landing card records in 2010 — leading to the Windrush scandal of 2018, when long-resident citizens were detained, deported or denied healthcare.

The Windrush brought around 1,000 passengers total, including Jamaicans returning from RAF service.
items.why: Right of abode in Britain has been redefined repeatedly. The 1948-1973 period when Commonwealth citizens had unrestricted entry is bracketed by very different regimes — and the 2018 scandal shows what happens when administrative memory fails.

items.title: Edward Jenner did not invent inoculation
items.claim: What did Edward Jenner demonstrate in 1796?

options.text: The first prevention of smallpox in human history
That deliberate infection with cowpox (vaccinia) protected against smallpox — a safer alternative to existing variolation (deliberate infection with smallpox itself)
The germ theory of disease
That smallpox could be cured after infection

items.reveal:
Variolation — inoculation with smallpox itself — was practised in China, India, the Ottoman Empire and West Africa centuries before Jenner. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu brought it to Britain from Constantinople in 1721. It worked but killed around 1-2% of those treated.

Jenner's experiment on 14 May 1796 used pus from milkmaid Sarah Nelmes's cowpox sores, inoculated into 8-year-old James Phipps. Phipps was later challenged with smallpox and did not become ill.

Jenner published in 1798. The Vaccination Act 1853 made it compulsory in England. WHO declared smallpox eradicated on 8 May 1980.
items.why: The 'lone genius' narrative misses preceding practice. Jenner improved a known technique with a safer biological substitute — major progress, but not the first prevention.

items.title: The NHS opened on 5 July 1948 — over GP opposition
items.claim: Did the medical profession support the founding of the NHS?

options.text: Yes, the BMA welcomed it unanimously
No — most GPs initially opposed it, fearing loss of independence; Aneurin Bevan, Minister of Health, said he had 'stuffed their mouths with gold' by allowing private practice within the NHS
The medical profession was indifferent
Bevan banned all private practice

items.reveal:
A 1948 BMA poll found around 90% of doctors opposed to entering the NHS. Bevan negotiated: GPs would be self-employed contractors, not salaried employees; consultants could have NHS posts plus private patients; teaching hospitals retained boards.

The Beveridge Report (1942) had set out the framework — slaying the 'five giants' of want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness. The Labour government (1945-1951) implemented the welfare state. The NHS launched on 5 July 1948, the same day as National Insurance and the National Assistance Act.

Bevan resigned in 1951 over the introduction of prescription charges for dental and optical services.
items.why: Major institutions are rarely born from consensus. The NHS as a 'national treasure' obscures its messy founding — contested, negotiated, and quickly amended.

items.title: McCarthy was censured by his own Senate in 1954
items.claim: How did Joseph McCarthy's anti-communist campaign end?

options.text: He was elected President
After televised Army-McCarthy hearings exposed his methods, the Senate voted 67-22 to censure him on 2 December 1954; he died of liver failure in 1957 aged 48
He was assassinated in 1955
He resigned and joined the Republican Party leadership

items.reveal:
McCarthy had risen on a 1950 Wheeling speech claiming 205 communists in the State Department. The Army-McCarthy hearings (April-June 1954) were televised; Army counsel Joseph Welch's 'Have you no sense of decency, sir?' on 9 June became the iconic moment.

Edward R. Murrow's CBS broadcast 'See It Now' on 9 March 1954 had already turned mainstream opinion. The Senate censure vote followed in December.

HUAC (House Un-American Activities Committee), the Hollywood blacklist, loyalty oaths and the Smith Act prosecutions continued separately and outlasted McCarthy.
items.why: McCarthyism as a phenomenon was bigger than McCarthy. His fall did not end the Red Scare — but it ended one specific style of grandstanding accusation, and television was central to both his rise and fall.

items.title: The Korean War killed around 3 million people
items.claim: What was the death toll of the Korean War (June 1950-July 1953)?

options.text: Around 100,000 — largely a limited conflict
Estimates centre around 3 million dead, mostly Korean civilians; nearly 37,000 US, around 1,000 British and Commonwealth, and over 400,000 Chinese troops killed
Around 500,000 total combatants only
Comparable to WWI losses for the Allies

items.reveal:
North Korea invaded south of the 38th parallel on 25 June 1950. UN forces under General MacArthur landed at Inchon (September 1950) and pushed to the Yalu River; China entered in October-November.

The armistice was signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953. There has never been a peace treaty — the two Koreas are still technically at war. Pyongyang was reduced by US bombing to perhaps 25% of its buildings; an estimated 20% of North Korea's population died.

In the US, sandwiched between WWII and Vietnam, it became 'the forgotten war' despite high casualties.
items.why: Conflict casualties are not just about combatant deaths. Korea's civilian toll, the bombing intensity and the legacy of an unresolved war shape East Asia today — but rarely feature in Cold War textbooks.

items.title: The US Vietnam draft was decided by a televised lottery
items.claim: How was the Vietnam draft (Selective Service) administered after 1969?

options.text: Strict order by date of birth, alphabetical
On 1 December 1969, blue capsules with birthdates were drawn from a glass jar on national TV — men born on dates drawn first were called up first
By voluntary enlistment only after 1969
By state quota with each state choosing its own method

items.reveal:
The 1 December 1969 lottery selected 19-26 year olds. 366 capsules (one per birthday including 29 February) were drawn live. Men with low numbers (1-195) were called; high numbers (typically 196+) were spared.

The statistical method was later shown to have biased the draw — capsules added in order from January were less thoroughly mixed, so December birthdays were over-represented at low numbers.

Deferments before 1969 — for university students, for medical reasons — disproportionately spared the wealthy. Around 2.7 million Americans served in Vietnam; 58,220 died. The draft ended in 1973.
items.why: Even apparently neutral mechanisms encode injustice. The Vietnam draft's class bias before 1969, and the statistical bias of the 1969 lottery itself, are case studies in how 'fairness' breaks down in practice.

items.title: Brown v Board did not desegregate schools quickly
items.claim: After Brown v Board of Education (17 May 1954), how fast did Southern schools desegregate?

options.text: Within months, all states complied

Massive resistance — by 1964, only around 2% of black students in the Deep South attended desegregated schools; federal enforcement came only with the Civil Rights Act 1964 and court orders into the 1970s
It applied only to Kansas and was ignored elsewhere
Northern schools refused but the South complied

items.reveal:
Brown II (1955) ordered desegregation 'with all deliberate speed' — an ambiguous phrase that licensed delay. The Southern Manifesto (March 1956), signed by 101 Congressmen, pledged resistance. Virginia closed schools in some counties (Prince Edward) rather than integrate.

Little Rock Nine (September 1957) needed federal troops. James Meredith at Ole Miss (1962) needed federal marshals. The Civil Rights Act 1964 and the Elementary and Secondary Education Act 1965 finally provided enforcement tools.

By some measures, US schools were more racially integrated in the late 1980s than they are now (Gary Orfield, UCLA Civil Rights Project).
items.why: Court rulings do not implement themselves. Brown is rightly celebrated but the gap between the 1954 decision and effective desegregation — 15+ years — shows how much enforcement and political will matter.

items.title: MLK's 'I have a dream' was largely improvised
items.claim: On 28 August 1963, King's speech at the Lincoln Memorial included the famous refrain. How did it enter the speech?

options.text: It was the title and central image of the prepared text
The prepared text did not include the dream section — Mahalia Jackson called out 'Tell them about the dream, Martin!' and he set his notes aside
He delivered the speech entirely from memory with no notes
The 'dream' lines were added by an aide after delivery

items.reveal:
King had used the 'dream' rhetoric earlier in 1963 (Detroit, June). His Washington text, drafted with Clarence Jones and Stanley Levison, ended differently. About 11 minutes in, gospel singer Mahalia Jackson — sitting behind him — reportedly called out the prompt. The next eight minutes were extemporaneous.

The March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom drew around 250,000 people. The Civil Rights Act passed the following year; the Voting Rights Act in 1965.

FBI surveillance of King intensified after the speech. J. Edgar Hoover called him 'the most dangerous Negro' in America.
items.why: The most quoted lines of 20th-century American speech-making were unscripted. Great rhetorical moments are often the product of preparation plus improvisation — not just the written page.

items.title: Weimar Germany had a 'golden' decade — but it was built on US loans
items.claim: Why did Weimar's relative stability (1924-1929) collapse?

options.text: Hitler's takeover began in 1924
The Dawes Plan (1924) restructured reparations with US loans; the Wall Street Crash (October 1929) collapsed lending; Stresemann had died in October 1929; unemployment hit 6 million by 1932
France invaded again in 1928
The British naval blockade resumed in 1927

items.reveal:
The Dawes Plan (1924) and Young Plan (1929) refinanced German reparations through US bank loans. Germany used the loans for infrastructure, social housing and reparations payments — a circular flow.

Gustav Stresemann's diplomacy (Locarno 1925, German League membership 1926) normalised relations with the West. He died on 3 October 1929, three weeks before the Wall Street Crash.

When US loans dried up, German banks failed (Danatbank, July 1931); unemployment soared; the Nazis went from 12 seats (1928) to 230 seats (July 1932), becoming the largest party.
items.why: Weimar's 'collapse' was not inevitable but was structurally vulnerable. The Crash was an external shock that destroyed a recovery dependent on foreign credit — a useful case in how interconnected economies fail.

items.title: Keynes resigned from the British delegation over Versailles
items.claim: What was Keynes's role at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference?

options.text: He helped draft the reparations clauses
He was a British Treasury official; he resigned in June 1919 in protest and published 'The Economic Consequences of the Peace' in December — arguing reparations would devastate Germany and Europe
He was not present at the conference
He represented Lloyd George as foreign affairs adviser

items.reveal:
Keynes was deputy to the British Treasury delegation. His book (December 1919) accused the Big Four — especially Clemenceau and Wilson — of imposing a 'Carthaginian peace' that would ensure future conflict.

The book sold over 100,000 copies and shaped Anglo-American opinion. It helped frame the 1930s 'appeasement' logic — Germany had been wronged at Versailles and deserved revision. Historians (notably Margaret MacMillan, 'Peacemakers' 2001) have argued Keynes overstated reparations' impact: Germany paid only a fraction.

Reparations were formally cancelled in 1932 (Lausanne).
items.why: Keynes's pamphlet is itself a historical event. It shaped the inter-war policy world more than the treaty article it attacked — a reminder that narratives of treaties can matter more than treaty texts.

items.title: British women got the vote in two instalments: 1918 and 1928
items.claim: When did UK women win equal voting rights with men?

options.text: 1918 — full equal franchise immediately after WWI
1918 gave the vote to women over 30 meeting property qualifications (around 8.4 million); 1928 (Equal Franchise Act) gave it to all women over 21 on the same terms as men
1832 (Great Reform Act)
1945 after WWII

items.reveal:
The Representation of the People Act 1918 enfranchised women over 30 who were householders, married to householders, occupiers of property at £5+ rent or university graduates. Men got the vote at 21 (or 19 if a serviceman).

The WSPU (Pankhursts, 1903), the NUWSS (Millicent Fawcett, constitutionalist) and women's war work all contributed. The 1918 compromise was partly designed to keep women a minority of the electorate.

The Equal Franchise Act 1928 gave women the vote at 21 on the same terms as men. Emmeline Pankhurst died on 14 June 1928, weeks before it took effect.
items.why: Reform is rarely complete in one step. The 10-year gap between 1918 and 1928 is itself part of the history — a partial victory deliberately designed to limit female political weight.

items.title: British abolition came in two acts, decades apart
items.claim: When did Britain abolish slavery?

options.text: 1807 — both the trade and slavery itself

The Slave Trade Act 1807 abolished the trade; the Slavery Abolition Act 1833 ended slavery in most British colonies from August 1834 — with £20 million paid in compensation to slave-owners, not the enslaved
1833 — both the trade and slavery
Magna Carta 1215

items.reveal:
The 1833 Act freed around 800,000 people in the Caribbean, Mauritius and the Cape from 1 August 1834. Field workers became 'apprentices' for six years (ended in 1838 after protests). Around 46,000 claims paid out £20 million — roughly 40% of the Treasury's annual budget.

The loan to finance the compensation (UCL's 'Legacies of British Slave-ownership' project) was only paid off by the UK Treasury in 2015. Slavery in British India was not covered by the 1833 Act; the Indian Slavery Act 1843 followed.

Wilberforce died on 29 July 1833, three days after the Act passed the Commons.
items.why: Abolition is celebrated as moral progress. The financial mechanics — owners compensated, the enslaved given six more years of forced labour, taxpayers paying off the loan until 2015 — complicate the story without erasing it.

items.title: The Great Reform Act 1832 added only about 200,000 voters
items.claim: How dramatic was the 1832 Reform Act's franchise extension?

options.text: It enfranchised all men over 21
It increased the electorate from around 400,000 to around 650,000 (roughly 1 in 7 adult males), redistributed seats from 'rotten boroughs' to industrial cities, and explicitly excluded women
It removed all voting restrictions for property
It introduced the secret ballot

items.reveal:
Old Sarum (one of the most notorious rotten boroughs) had no inhabitants but returned two MPs. Manchester, Birmingham and Leeds had none. The 1832 Act abolished 56 small boroughs and gave seats to industrial centres.

The £10 householder franchise in boroughs admitted urban middle-class voters; the 40-shilling freeholder in counties remained. Women were explicitly excluded for the first time (previously they had been excluded by custom).

The Second Reform Act (1867, Disraeli) added urban working-class men; the Third (1884, Gladstone) extended this to county householders. Adult male suffrage came only in 1918.
items.why: 'Great' reform was incremental. The 1832 Act is correctly remembered as a turning point — but as a beginning, not a conclusion. The disappointment fuelled Chartism (1838-1858) and the long campaign that followed.

items.title: Jefferson's draft Declaration condemned slavery — Congress cut it
items.claim: What happened to the anti-slavery clause in Jefferson's 1776 Declaration draft?

options.text: There was no such clause

Jefferson included a passage blaming the slave trade on George III ('he has waged cruel war against human nature itself'); the Continental Congress removed it under pressure from South Carolina and Georgia
It was added later by Adams and Franklin
It was kept but ignored in practice

items.reveal:
Jefferson's draft (June 1776) called slavery 'execrable commerce' and blamed George III for it — a strained legal claim, since the colonists themselves operated the trade. Jefferson himself enslaved over 600 people across his life.

The Continental Congress's edits removed the passage on 4 July. Jefferson later wrote his autobiography accusing 'our Southern brethren' of the cut, though Northern delegates also supported removal.

The 1808 expiration of the constitutional protection of the trade (article I section 9) finally allowed federal abolition of the Atlantic slave trade — though domestic slavery continued until the Thirteenth Amendment (1865).
items.why: Founding documents are political compromises. The American Revolution's promise of liberty had a slavery-shaped hole written into it by deliberate editorial decision — the contradiction that produced the Civil War 85 years later.

items.title: The Terror killed around 17,000 by guillotine — and many more by other means
items.claim: What was the human cost of the French Revolutionary Terror (September 1793-July 1794)?

options.text: Around 200 prominent executions only
Around 17,000 official executions (16,594 verified by Donald Greer), plus tens of thousands killed in the Vendée civil war and many more dying in prisons
Over a million executions
Confined to Paris, around 3,000 deaths

items.reveal:
Donald Greer's 1935 study 'The Incidence of the Terror' counted 16,594 official executions. The Vendée counter-revolution and its suppression killed perhaps 170,000-250,000. Around 200,000 were imprisoned during the Terror; thousands died in custody.

Robespierre fell on 9 Thermidor Year II (27 July 1794) and was guillotined the next day — the wave he had ridden turned. The guillotine had been adopted in 1792 as a humane, egalitarian execution method.

The Bourbon Restoration (1814) and Napoleon III's regime committed their own political killings; the Paris Commune's suppression (1871) killed perhaps 10,000-20,000 in a week.
items.why: Death tolls determine how a revolution is remembered. The Terror's official 17,000 was orders of magnitude smaller than the Vendée suppression — but the urban, named victims shape memory.

items.title: Enclosure transferred millions of acres to private hands
items.claim: How much land was affected by Parliamentary enclosure (c. 1750-1850)?

options.text: Around 100,000 acres total
Around 7 million acres — roughly a fifth of England — was enclosed by some 4,000 individual Acts of Parliament between 1750 and 1850
Enclosure was rare and ended in the 16th century
Only royal forests were enclosed

items.reveal:
Earlier enclosure (16th-17th centuries) had been informal and contested (Kett's Rebellion 1549). Parliamentary enclosure required individual Acts, with commissioners surveying and reallocating land in compact private holdings.

Common rights to graze, gather wood, glean and forage were extinguished. J. L. and Barbara Hammond's 'The Village Labourer' (1911) emphasised dispossession; later historians (J. M. Neeson, 'Commoners' 1993) revived the case for serious social impact.

The General Enclosure Acts of 1801 and 1845 streamlined the process. By 1900 the English commons were almost gone — though the Commons Preservation Society (1865) saved spaces like Hampstead Heath and Epping Forest.
items.why: The transition to industrial capitalism had a rural component. Enclosure freed up labour for cities and consolidated land for improved farming — at the cost of displacing a way of life that contemporaries actually missed.

items.title: Prohibition created modern organised crime in America
items.claim: What did Prohibition (1920-1933) actually do to alcohol consumption and crime?

options.text: It successfully eliminated alcohol consumption

Consumption fell initially but rose again; it transferred a major industry to organised criminals (Al Capone, Lucky Luciano), corrupted police and politicians, and was repealed by the 21st Amendment in December 1933
It was repealed within a year as a failure
It applied only to spirits, not beer or wine

items.reveal:
The 18th Amendment (ratified January 1919) and Volstead Act (October 1919) banned the manufacture, sale and transport of 'intoxicating liquors'. Domestic consumption was not banned; medicinal whiskey, sacramental wine and home cider remained legal.

Al Capone's Chicago Outfit reportedly grossed $100 million a year by 1927. The St Valentine's Day Massacre (14 February 1929) shocked the public. Federal income from alcohol taxes had been about 30% of federal revenue before Prohibition — its loss became politically painful during the Depression.

The 21st Amendment (December 1933) is the only constitutional amendment to repeal another.
items.why: Banning a popular consumption good creates the conditions for an illegal industry. The lesson — visible in 20th-century drug policy and elsewhere — was already clear in 1933 but is endlessly relearned.

items.title: Unemployment in the US Depression peaked at 25%
items.claim: How bad was the Great Depression in the US?

options.text: Unemployment peaked at about 10%
Unemployment peaked at around 25% (around 13 million) in 1933; GDP fell by roughly 30% from 1929-1933; thousands of banks failed
It was a brief recession lasting only a year
Unemployment never reached 5%

items.reveal_title: A quarter of workers without jobs
items.reveal:
The Wall Street Crash began on Black Thursday (24 October 1929) and Black Tuesday (29 October). The Federal Reserve's contractionary response is blamed by economic historians (Friedman and Schwartz, Bernanke) for deepening the slump.

FDR took office on 4 March 1933 with around 13 million unemployed and 9,000 banks closed. The First Hundred Days produced the Emergency Banking Act, the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), the Agricultural Adjustment Act (AAA), the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) and the National Industrial Recovery Act (NIRA).

Unemployment was still around 14% in 1940. Full recovery came only with WWII spending.
items.why: The New Deal is sometimes credited with ending the Depression. Statistically, it lifted the worst but did not restore full employment. War mobilisation did that — an awkward fact for both 'New Deal worked' and 'New Deal failed' narratives.

items.title: Hastings lasted nearly a full day and was won by a feigned retreat
items.claim: The Battle of Hastings (14 October 1066) is often remembered as a swift Norman triumph. What actually happened?

options.text: William routed Harold's army within an hour
Fighting lasted from around 9 a.m. to dusk; the Anglo-Saxon shield-wall held until Norman cavalry used feigned retreats to draw housecarls down Senlac Hill, exposing the line
The English never engaged — they fled at the sight of Norman cavalry
The battle was decided by a single cavalry charge at dawn

items.reveal_title: A near thing on Senlac Hill
items.reveal:
William of Poitiers and the Bayeux Tapestry both record the day-long fight. Harold's army held the high ground in a shield-wall formation; William's archers, infantry and cavalry attacked uphill. A rumour that William had died spread early; he raised his helmet to show his face and rally his troops.

The feigned retreats — possibly accidental at first, then deliberate — broke the discipline of the shield-wall. Harold was killed late in the day along with his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine.

William was not crowned at Westminster until 25 December 1066. Anglo-Saxon resistance continued for years (the Harrying of the North, 1069-70).
items.why: 1066 looks decisive in retrospect. On the day it was a hill-defence that nearly held — and might have, if not for a tactical innovation. Contingency in military history.

items.title: The Spanish Armada was defeated partly by the weather
items.claim: How was the Spanish Armada (1588) actually defeated?

options.text: An English naval victory in a single set-piece battle

English fireships at Calais broke the Armada's crescent formation; Gravelines (8 August) inflicted damage; storms in the North Sea and around Scotland and Ireland wrecked perhaps half the surviving ships on the journey home
The Armada turned back before reaching England
Drake destroyed it in a night attack at Cadiz

items.reveal:
The Armada of around 130 ships, led by the Duke of Medina Sidonia, sailed up the Channel in a defensive crescent. Lord Howard of Effingham and Sir Francis Drake harried it but failed to break the formation in open water. On the night of 7-8 August, fireships at Calais panicked the Spanish into cutting their cables.

The Battle of Gravelines (8 August) damaged several galleons. The fleet was driven north into the North Sea; storms around Scotland and the west coast of Ireland wrecked perhaps 35-50 ships. Around 15,000 Spaniards died, mostly from disease, drowning and shipwreck — not English gunfire.

Elizabeth I's commemorative medal read 'Flavit Deus et dissipati sunt' — 'God blew and they were scattered.'
items.why: National myths simplify. The English fleet performed creditably but did not destroy the Armada in battle — wind and disease did most of the killing. The Protestant providential frame was political branding.

items.title: The Great Plague of London killed around 100,000 in 1665
items.claim: How severe was the Great Plague of 1665?

options.text: Around 1,000 deaths concentrated in one parish
Around 100,000 dead — roughly a quarter of London's population — recorded through the Bills of Mortality from spring 1665 to early 1666
No reliable count exists from the period
The plague affected only beggars

items.reveal:
The Bills of Mortality recorded plague deaths weekly. The peak week (12-19 September 1665) recorded over 7,000 plague deaths in London. Houses where plague was found were marked with a red cross and 'Lord have mercy upon us', with inhabitants sealed inside for 40 days.

Wealthy Londoners fled to the country, including Charles II's court (to Oxford). Samuel Pepys remained and recorded the empty streets in his diary. The village of Eyam in Derbyshire voluntarily quarantined itself in 1665-66 after plague arrived in a bale of cloth from London.

The Great Fire of September 1666 is sometimes credited with ending the plague — modern historians are sceptical; the outbreak was already declining and rats were reinfested elsewhere.
items.why: Plague returned to England in waves long after the medieval Black Death. The 1665 outbreak was the last major one — and the social mechanisms (quarantine, flight, recording) prefigure modern public-health responses.

items.title: The Royal Society was founded in 1660 with a royal charter from Charles II
items.claim: What is the Royal Society and when was it founded?

options.text: A medieval guild of physicians
A learned society for natural philosophy founded 28 November 1660, granted royal charters by Charles II in 1662 and 1663, with the motto 'Nullius in verba' ('take nobody's word for it')
A 19th-century invention of the Victorians
A department of the College of Arms

items.reveal:
Twelve men met at Gresham College, London, on 28 November 1660 after a lecture by Christopher Wren, to form 'a Colledge for the Promoting of Physico-Mathematicall Experimentall Learning'. Early members included Robert Boyle, Robert Hooke (curator of experiments), John Wilkins and Wren.

The motto 'Nullius in verba' (taken from Horace) signalled commitment to experiment over authority. The Philosophical Transactions, first published in 1665, is the world's oldest continuously published scientific journal.

Isaac Newton served as President from 1703 until his death in 1727. Charles II reportedly mocked the society for 'weighing air'.
items.why: Modern science as an institutional practice has a specific founding moment. The 1660 Restoration created intellectual breathing space for a society that has shaped global science ever since.

items.title: The abolition campaign invented modern political organising
items.claim: How did the 18th-century abolition movement work?

options.text: Wilberforce campaigned alone in Parliament

Mass petitions (1788 saw over 100 petitions with around 60,000 signatures), a sugar boycott by perhaps 300,000 households (1791-92), the Brookes ship diagram, public lectures by Clarkson, Equiano's autobiography (1789) — a prototype of modern campaigning
It relied solely on Quaker petitions
It was an underground secret movement

items.reveal:
Thomas Clarkson rode an estimated 35,000 miles gathering evidence and lecturing. Olaudah Equiano's 'Interesting Narrative' (1789) sold widely and gave testimony from a formerly enslaved African.

Josiah Wedgwood's 1787 medallion 'Am I Not a Man and a Brother?' became one of the first political logos. The diagram of the slave ship Brookes (1788) showed enslaved people packed into a hold — a mass-circulated visual that shocked public opinion.

The sugar boycott urged consumers to use East India rather than West India sugar; some sugar bowls were sold inscribed 'East India sugar not made by slaves'. Pressure on Parliament built across two decades before the 1807 Act.
items.why: The toolkit of modern protest — petitions, boycotts, visual propaganda, celebrity testimony — was assembled by the abolition campaign. Its 50-year arc to the 1833 Act is a template for sustained reform politics.

items.title: Edwin Chadwick's 1842 report drove the 1848 Public Health Act
items.claim: What was the immediate origin of British public health legislation?

options.text: A spontaneous parliamentary initiative without prior research

Edwin Chadwick's 'Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population' (1842) documented appalling urban conditions; the cholera epidemic of 1848-49 (around 53,000 dead in England and Wales) prompted the Public Health Act 1848 creating the General Board of Health and local boards
Disraeli's 1875 Act was the first such law
The 1848 Act applied only to Scotland

items.reveal:
Chadwick was a Poor Law commissioner and disciple of Jeremy Bentham. His report, partly self-funded, argued that disease and poverty were linked to environmental conditions — drains, water, ventilation, cesspits.

The 1848 Public Health Act was permissive: local boards could be established by petition or where mortality exceeded 23 per 1,000. The 1875 Public Health Act under Disraeli made provisions compulsory and gave local authorities effective powers over water, sewers, housing, food and nuisance.

John Simon (chief medical officer from 1855) institutionalised the role of medical officers of health across the country.
items.why: Modern state public health did not begin with the NHS. It began with sanitarian engineers and statisticians in the 1840s-70s, who treated mortality data as a political argument.

items.title: Alexander the Great died at 32 with no clear successor
items.claim: What happened to Alexander's empire after his death in 323 BCE?

options.text: It passed peacefully to his infant son

Alexander died in Babylon on 10 or 11 June 323 BCE aged 32; his generals (the Diadochi) fought 40 years of wars (323-281 BCE) carving the empire into Hellenistic kingdoms — Ptolemaic Egypt, Seleucid Asia, Antigonid Macedon
Rome immediately conquered it
It dissolved into independent Greek city-states again

items.reveal:
Alexander had conquered from Macedonia to the Indus in 13 years. Asked on his deathbed who should succeed him, he reportedly said 'to the strongest' (some sources say 'Krateros'). His half-brother Philip III Arrhidaeus (mentally disabled) and posthumous son Alexander IV were both murdered within years.

The Wars of the Diadochi — Antigonus, Ptolemy, Seleucus, Lysimachus, Cassander — produced the Hellenistic world that lasted until Rome absorbed it (Macedon 146 BCE, the Seleucid rump 64 BCE, Ptolemaic Egypt 30 BCE).

The Hellenistic kingdoms spread Greek language and culture across western Asia and Egypt — the koine Greek of the New Testament is a downstream consequence.
items.why: Empires built by single conquerors rarely outlast them. Alexander's death at 32 is one of the great 'what ifs' — but his empire's fracture is also a structural fact about charismatic rule without institutional succession.

items.title: The Berlin Wall fell partly because of a press-conference error
items.claim: How did the Berlin Wall come to open on 9 November 1989?

options.text: Soviet troops dismantled it overnight on Gorbachev's orders

East German official Günter Schabowski announced new travel rules at a 6 p.m. press conference; asked when they took effect, he said 'as far as I know, immediately'; East Berliners massed at checkpoints and crossings opened without orders
Mass armed insurrection overwhelmed border guards
West German forces breached the wall by force

items.reveal:
The East German politburo had agreed new travel rules on 9 November 1989, intended to take effect the following day with bureaucratic processing. Schabowski had not been briefed in detail. Asked by Italian journalist Riccardo Ehrman 'when does this take effect?', he shuffled papers and said 'Sofort, unverzüglich' — immediately, without delay.

Within hours East Berliners gathered at the Bornholmer Strasse crossing. Commander Harald Jäger received no orders and, faced with thousands of citizens, opened the barrier around 11.30 p.m.
