Within months the regime collapsed. German reunification followed on 3 October 1990. The Soviet Union itself dissolved on 26 December 1991.
items.why: Major historical turning points can hinge on a botched press conference. The Wall's opening was not authorised in the way it happened — it was triggered by a misstatement that the crowd then made real.

items.title: Pope Urban II launched the First Crusade in 1095
items.claim: What did Pope Urban II do at the Council of Clermont on 27 November 1095?

options.text: He banned all warfare among Christians
He called on Western Christians to take the cross and recover Jerusalem from the Seljuk Turks, offering remission of sin to those who fought — launching what became the First Crusade (1096-99)
He excommunicated all kings of Europe
He convened only to discuss church reform

items.reveal:
Urban's speech at Clermont survives in four contemporary versions, all written years later. The crowd reportedly responded 'Deus vult!' — God wills it. The motive came partly from the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos's appeal for help after Seljuk advances after the Battle of Manzikert (1071).

The First Crusade (1096-99) captured Antioch (1098) and Jerusalem (15 July 1099) after a massacre of inhabitants. Crusader states (Edessa, Antioch, Tripoli, the Kingdom of Jerusalem) were established.

Subsequent crusades (Second 1147-49, Third 1189-92, Fourth sacked Constantinople 1204) showed the institution's instability. Jerusalem fell to Saladin in 1187. The last Crusader holding, Acre, fell in 1291.
items.why: The Crusades were a centuries-long phenomenon launched by a single papal speech that promised salvation for warfare. The collision they began (Western Christianity, Byzantine Christianity, Islam, Judaism) reshaped the medieval Mediterranean.

items.title: Athenian democracy excluded most of the population
items.claim: How inclusive was 5th-century BCE Athenian democracy?

options.text: All inhabitants over 18 could vote

Citizen-men over 18 (perhaps 30,000-40,000) voted in the assembly (ekklesia); women, slaves (perhaps 80,000-100,000) and metics (resident foreigners, perhaps 25,000) had no political rights — citizens were probably 10-20% of the city's population
Women had equal political rights with men
Slaves voted as freed men

items.reveal:
The Athenian assembly met around 40 times a year on the Pnyx hill. Decisions on war, treaties and major legislation required a quorum of around 6,000. The Council of 500 (boule), juries and most magistracies were filled by lot — a feature of radical democracy.

Pericles' citizenship law (451 BCE) restricted citizenship to those with two Athenian parents. Aristotle's 'Athenaion Politeia' (4th century BCE) describes the system. Thucydides records Pericles' Funeral Oration extolling Athenian democracy in 431 BCE.

Women, even citizen-women, had no vote. Slaves performed much of the manual labour that supported leisure for political participation.
items.why: Calling Athens 'the cradle of democracy' is true with major qualifications. Its political innovations were real and influential — but its exclusions were severe enough that modern democracies share aspirations more than they share institutions with it.

items.title: Caesar's assassins included his own protégés
items.claim: Who killed Julius Caesar on 15 March 44 BCE?

options.text: Foreign agents acting for Parthia
A conspiracy of around 60 senators, led by Marcus Junius Brutus (who Caesar had pardoned and promoted) and Gaius Cassius Longinus, stabbed him 23 times in Pompey's Theatre
Mark Antony alone, in a private quarrel
He died of natural causes; the assassination is a later invention

items.reveal:
Caesar had crossed the Rubicon in January 49 BCE, defeated Pompey at Pharsalus (48), and been declared dictator perpetuo in February 44 BCE. The conspirators feared a return to monarchy.

The assassination took place at a Senate meeting at the Curia of Pompey. Suetonius and Plutarch describe the scene; the famous 'Et tu, Brute?' is Shakespeare's. Plutarch records Caesar saying 'kai su, teknon?' ('you too, child?') in Greek to Brutus.

The Liberators expected to restore the Republic. Instead they triggered the Liberators' civil war, ending at Philippi (42 BCE) with Brutus's suicide. Octavian became Augustus, first emperor, in 27 BCE — the Republic was over.
items.why: Assassinations rarely produce the political outcome the assassins want. The Liberators killed to save the Republic and accelerated its end — a paradox of political violence visible across history.

items.title: The Western Roman Empire 'fell' in 476 CE with little fanfare
items.claim: What happened in 476 CE?

options.text: Rome was sacked and destroyed in a single battle

The Germanic warlord Odoacer deposed the last Western emperor, Romulus Augustulus (a boy of about 16), and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople — contemporaries barely noticed; the date was made significant by later historians
The Senate voted to dissolve the empire
Rome converted to Christianity in 476

items.reveal:
The Western Empire had been declining for over a century — barbarian federate settlements, Visigothic sack of Rome (410 under Alaric), Vandal sack (455), shrinking tax base, military commanders of barbarian origin holding real power. Romulus Augustulus, installed by his general father Orestes in October 475, was deposed by Odoacer on 4 September 476.

Odoacer ruled as king of Italy under nominal Byzantine sovereignty. The Eastern Empire continued until 1453. Edward Gibbon's 'Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire' (1776-89) made 476 the canonical end date.

Modern historians (Peter Heather, Bryan Ward-Perkins, Walter Goffart) debate whether 476 marks 'fall', 'transformation' or simply 'continued change'.
items.why: 'The fall of Rome' is a label imposed centuries later on a gradual process. The boundary between antiquity and the Middle Ages is a periodisation choice — useful for teaching, misleading if treated as a single event.

items.title: Thomas Becket was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral in 1170
items.claim: What happened on 29 December 1170?

options.text: Becket died of natural causes during a service

Four knights of Henry II — Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy, Richard le Breton — murdered Archbishop Becket in Canterbury Cathedral after Henry's outburst 'Will no one rid me of this turbulent priest?'
He was assassinated in Paris
He was executed for treason after a public trial

items.reveal:
Becket and Henry had clashed for years over the jurisdiction of church courts (Constitutions of Clarendon, 1164). Becket had fled to France, returned in 1170, and excommunicated bishops who had supported Henry. The king's exact words are disputed but the four knights took them as licence.

Becket was canonised in 1173. Henry II did public penance at Canterbury in 1174, walking barefoot and being scourged by monks. The shrine became one of medieval Europe's major pilgrimage sites — the setting of Chaucer's 'Canterbury Tales' (1380s).

Henry VIII destroyed the shrine in 1538 during the Dissolution.
items.why: Church-state conflict was the defining political question of high medieval Europe. Becket's murder dramatised the limits of royal power over the church — and made Canterbury a centre of European devotion for 350 years.

items.title: Joan of Arc was burned at Rouen in 1431, aged 19
items.claim: What did Joan of Arc achieve before her execution?

options.text: Nothing — her story is later legend

She convinced Charles VII she had divine guidance, led French forces to relieve the siege of Orléans in May 1429, helped recover Reims and have Charles crowned (July 1429); captured by Burgundians, sold to the English, tried for heresy and burned at Rouen on 30 May 1431
She was a Burgundian general who switched sides
She was canonised within months of her death

items.reveal:
Joan was a peasant from Domrémy who claimed visions of St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret from age 13. After persuading Charles's court at Chinon, she joined the relief of Orléans aged 17. The siege was lifted in nine days; Reims (the traditional coronation city) was retaken; Charles VII was crowned on 17 July 1429.

She was captured at Compiègne (May 1430), held for ransom by the Burgundians, sold to the English, and tried by a French ecclesiastical court at Rouen. The trial of 1455-56 (after the English left) annulled the conviction. She was canonised in 1920.

The Hundred Years War ended in French victory at Castillon (1453).
items.why: The Hundred Years War's turning point is a teenager with no military training. Joan of Arc's trial transcripts survive — she remains one of the most documented medieval figures and a case in how religion, war and gender intersect.

items.title: Thomas More's 'Utopia' (1516) coined the word
items.claim: What did Thomas More publish in 1516?

options.text: A history of the Wars of the Roses

'Utopia' — a Latin work describing a fictional island society, coining the word from Greek 'ou-topos' (no place) and 'eu-topos' (good place); a humanist critique of European politics, property and religion
A defence of the medieval feudal system
A translation of the Quran

items.reveal_title: No place that critiques every place
items.reveal:
'Utopia' was written in Latin and first printed at Louvain in 1516. The Utopians hold property in common, work six hours a day, practise religious toleration and choose elected officials. The book mixes serious proposal with deliberate ambiguity — More may or may not endorse his fictional society.

More was Lord Chancellor under Henry VIII from 1529 to 1532, resigning over the king's annulment plans. He refused the Oath of Succession (1534) and was executed on 6 July 1535 with the famous 'King's good servant, but God's first.'

He was canonised in 1935. The word 'utopia' entered every European language as a term for an imagined ideal society.
items.why: Renaissance humanism produced political ideas centuries ahead of their reception. 'Utopia' has been read by socialists, anarchists, Catholics and modern progressives — each finding their own programme in More's deliberately ambiguous text.

items.title: The Spinning Jenny multiplied a worker's output eightfold
items.claim: What did James Hargreaves invent around 1764?

options.text: The steam engine
The Spinning Jenny — a multi-spindle frame allowing one operator to spin eight (later up to 120) threads at once; patented 1770, transformed cotton production
The cotton gin
The shipping container

items.reveal:
Hargreaves, a Lancashire weaver, named the device after his daughter (or wife) Jenny. Early versions had 8 spindles; later models up to 120. Cotton output per worker rose dramatically.

The jenny was joined by Richard Arkwright's water frame (1769, water-powered) and Samuel Crompton's mule (1779, combining both). Edmund Cartwright's power loom (1785) mechanised weaving. Eli Whitney's cotton gin (1793) mechanised seed-removal in the US South — increasing cotton supply and intensifying slavery.

Lancashire became the centre of world cotton manufacture by 1830, employing perhaps half a million workers by mid-century. Cotton's raw material came largely from the slave plantations of the US South until the American Civil War.
items.why: The Industrial Revolution was a sequence of specific machines invented by specific people, each enabling the next. 'Cotton' is shorthand for a chain of innovation that links Lancashire mills to plantation slavery.

items.title: The 1833 Factory Act created the first state inspectorate
items.claim: What was the significance of the 1833 Factory Act?

options.text: It banned all factory work

It prohibited textile factory employment of children under 9, limited 9-13 year olds to 9 hours/day and 13-18 year olds to 12 hours, required two hours of schooling daily — and created four paid factory inspectors with powers of entry
It applied only to coal mines
It was repealed within a year

items.reveal:
Earlier factory acts (1802 Health and Morals of Apprentices Act, 1819 Cotton Mills Act) had been largely unenforced. The 1833 Act, drafted under Lord Althorp, created the first national factory inspectorate — a tiny force initially but a precedent for state enforcement of working conditions.

Lord Ashley (later 7th Earl of Shaftesbury) campaigned for the Ten Hours Movement, achieved in 1847 (Ten Hours Act). The Mines Act 1842 banned women and children underground.

The inspectors' annual reports — read by Marx in the British Museum — provided detailed evidence of factory conditions that shaped political argument for decades.
items.why: The modern regulatory state is built up Act by Act. The 1833 inspectorate is a small institutional innovation that became a template for state oversight of every industry that followed.

items.title: Constantinople fell to Ottoman cannons in 1453
items.claim: What ended the Byzantine Empire?

options.text: A Mongol invasion
Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II besieged Constantinople from 6 April; massive Hungarian-built cannons breached the Theodosian walls; the city fell on 29 May 1453, ending the 1,123-year Eastern Roman Empire
An Italian Crusade in 1453
A peaceful handover after negotiation

items.reveal:
Mehmed II, aged 21, had artillery cast by Orban, a Hungarian engineer — including the Basilic, around 8 metres long, firing stone balls of around 270 kg. The walls of Theodosius (built 5th century) had held for a thousand years; gunpowder ended their effectiveness.

Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos died in the fighting; his body was never identified. Around 7,000 Byzantine and Genoese defenders faced perhaps 80,000-150,000 Ottoman troops.

Mehmed converted Hagia Sophia into a mosque (it remained one until 1934, when Atatürk converted it to a museum; reconverted to a mosque in 2020). The fall pushed Greek scholars and texts west into Italy — fuel for the late Renaissance.
items.why: Military technology can end empires. The fall of Constantinople closes the medieval Mediterranean and marks a conventional boundary between medieval and early modern history.

items.title: Newton published the Principia in 1687
items.claim: What did Newton's Principia (1687) achieve?

options.text: A book of alchemical recipes

'Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica' set out three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation, deriving Kepler's planetary laws mathematically — uniting terrestrial and celestial physics
A defence of the Aristotelian universe
A treatise on biblical chronology only

items.reveal_title: Standing on the shoulders of giants
items.reveal:
The Principia was published in Latin in July 1687, funded by Edmond Halley after the Royal Society's stock of unsold fish books left it short of cash. Newton derived the inverse-square law of gravity, the three laws of motion, and applied them to planets, comets, the tides and the shape of the Earth.

Newton had developed calculus (his 'fluxions') in 1665-66 during the plague closure of Cambridge. He published Opticks in 1704 in English.

Newton became Master of the Mint in 1699, prosecuting counterfeiters. He served as President of the Royal Society from 1703 to 1727. His tomb is in Westminster Abbey.
items.why: Modern physics begins with one book. The unification of celestial and terrestrial mechanics in 1687 is the high-water mark of the Scientific Revolution — and remained the framework of physics until Einstein.

items.title: The Plague of Athens (430 BCE) killed perhaps a quarter of the population
items.claim: What was the Plague of Athens?

options.text: A modern Greek outbreak

An epidemic (possibly typhus, smallpox or typhoid — debated) hit Athens 430-426 BCE during the Peloponnesian War, killing perhaps 75,000-100,000 including Pericles; described in detail by Thucydides who survived the disease himself
A famine, not a disease
The same outbreak as the 1665 London plague

items.reveal:
Thucydides' 'History of the Peloponnesian War' (Book II) records the symptoms in clinical detail — fever, redness of the eyes, internal ulceration, severe thirst. He notes that survivors gained immunity. The cause remains debated; DNA evidence from Athenian mass graves (2006) tentatively suggested typhoid fever.

Pericles, the city's leading statesman, died of the plague in autumn 429 BCE. The disease wrecked Athenian morale and military capacity early in the war with Sparta, which Athens eventually lost in 404 BCE.

Thucydides is sometimes called 'the father of scientific history' — his account of the plague aimed to provide future generations with a description that would help them recognise it.
items.why: Ancient epidemics had political consequences. The death of Pericles changed the leadership of Athens at a critical moment; the disease's social effects — Thucydides describes breakdown of religious and legal norms — anticipate modern observations on epidemic societies.

items.title: The Korean War never formally ended
items.claim: How did the Korean War conclude?

options.text: With a peace treaty in 1953

An armistice signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953 by representatives of the UN Command, North Korea and China — but no peace treaty; the Koreas remain technically at war and the DMZ at the 38th parallel divides them
With Chinese troops withdrawing voluntarily
With reunification under South Korea

items.reveal:
Armistice negotiations began in July 1951 and lasted two years, largely over the issue of prisoner repatriation. South Korean President Syngman Rhee refused to sign and unilaterally released 27,000 North Korean POWs in June 1953.

The Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) is 4 km wide and around 250 km long — one of the most heavily militarised borders in the world. Periodic incidents (the 1968 capture of USS Pueblo, the 2010 Yeonpyeong shelling) keep the conflict warm.

Moves toward a formal peace declaration have repeatedly stalled. The Korean War cost around 3 million lives — Korean civilians the majority — and shaped East Asian security for over 70 years.
items.why: Unresolved conflicts shape decades. The absence of a Korean peace treaty in 1953 is the structural foundation of every subsequent crisis on the peninsula.

items.title: The Bay of Pigs invasion (April 1961) was a CIA-trained failure
items.claim: What happened at the Bay of Pigs?

options.text: A successful US Marine landing in Cuba

Around 1,400 CIA-trained Cuban exiles (Brigade 2506) landed at Bahía de Cochinos on 17 April 1961; without expected US air support, they were defeated within three days, with 114 killed and around 1,200 captured
A successful overthrow of Castro
A peaceful protest broken up by Castro's police

items.reveal:
The operation was planned under Eisenhower and inherited by Kennedy after his January 1961 inauguration. Kennedy cancelled the second air strike that would have neutralised Cuban air power. The exiles landed in swampy terrain with no popular uprising materialising.

Kennedy publicly accepted responsibility — 'success has many fathers, failure is an orphan' — and the CIA director Allen Dulles resigned. The prisoners were exchanged in December 1962 for $53 million of food and medicine.

The humiliation pushed Castro further toward the Soviet Union; Khrushchev's decision to place missiles in Cuba in 1962 followed directly. Operation Mongoose continued covert efforts against Castro through the 1960s.
items.why: Failed interventions can be more consequential than successful ones. The Bay of Pigs led directly to the Cuban Missile Crisis — and reshaped Cold War risk-taking for both sides.

items.title: The Cuban Missile Crisis lasted exactly 13 days
items.claim: What was the timeline of the Cuban Missile Crisis?

options.text: Several months of public negotiation
From U-2 photos showing missiles on 14 October to Khrushchev's announcement of withdrawal on 28 October 1962 — 13 days, with a US naval 'quarantine' announced 22 October
A single weekend of negotiations
Three years of standoff (1962-65)

items.reveal:
U-2 reconnaissance on 14 October 1962 photographed Soviet medium-range ballistic missile sites under construction in Cuba. Kennedy convened the Executive Committee (ExComm) which debated air strike, invasion or blockade.

Kennedy announced the 'quarantine' (a blockade by another name to avoid an act of war) on 22 October. On 27 October ('Black Saturday'), a U-2 was shot down over Cuba, killing pilot Rudolf Anderson — the only direct combat fatality.

Khrushchev announced withdrawal on 28 October, exchanging the public concession of US non-invasion of Cuba and the secret removal of Jupiter missiles from Turkey. The hotline between Washington and Moscow was installed in 1963.
items.why: The closest the Cold War came to nuclear war. The combination of intelligence, diplomacy and luck that produced the outcome is the most-studied case in international relations.

items.title: The Elizabethan Settlement (1559) was a deliberate compromise
items.claim: What did the Elizabethan Religious Settlement of 1559 establish?

options.text: Full Calvinist Protestantism

Act of Supremacy (Elizabeth as 'Supreme Governor' — softer than 'Supreme Head'); Act of Uniformity (revised 1559 Prayer Book); Thirty-Nine Articles (1571 final) — a deliberately broad 'via media' between Catholic and Reformed
Return to Roman Catholicism
Suspension of all religious practice

items.reveal:
Elizabeth's first Parliament (1559) produced the legislation by narrow margins — particularly the Act of Supremacy, opposed by all 18 surviving bishops from Mary's reign. The 1559 Prayer Book combined elements of Cranmer's 1549 and 1552 books, with deliberately ambiguous language on the Eucharist.

The Act of Uniformity required attendance at parish church on pain of fines. The Thirty-Nine Articles (1563, finalised 1571) defined Anglican doctrine. The Settlement was challenged by Puritans wanting further reform and by Catholic recusants.

Elizabeth reportedly said she would not 'open windows into men's souls' — outward conformity was required; private belief was largely left alone.
items.why: The Church of England's modern shape — episcopal, vernacular, broad — is a 1559 political compromise that became national habit over 45 years. One of the most successful exercises in deliberate ambiguity in European history.

items.title: Hieroglyphs were unreadable for 1,500 years until the Rosetta Stone
items.claim: How were Egyptian hieroglyphs deciphered?

options.text: They were always readable

Knowledge was lost by around 400 CE; the Rosetta Stone (a 196 BCE decree in hieroglyphic, demotic and Greek) was found by French soldiers near Rosetta in 1799 and Jean-François Champollion announced his decipherment in 1822
Napoleon personally deciphered them
They remain undeciphered today

items.reveal:
The Stone was found at Rosetta (Rashid) on 15 July 1799 by Pierre-François Bouchard during the French invasion of Egypt. The British captured it after Napoleon's defeat; it has been in the British Museum since 1802.

Champollion built on Thomas Young's earlier identification of phonetic elements in royal cartouches. On 14 September 1822 he wrote 'Je tiens mon affaire!' ('I've got it!') and fainted. He published the 'Lettre à M. Dacier' announcing the decipherment two weeks later.

The Stone records a decree of Ptolemy V issued at Memphis. Hieroglyphic, demotic (cursive Egyptian) and Greek versions allowed cross-comparison — Greek being a known language.
items.why: Civilisations can lose access to their own past. Ancient Egypt was readable to scholars within decades of 1822 — and the rediscovery transformed European understanding of the ancient world.

items.title: The Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron enforced the 1807 ban
items.claim: How was the 1807 abolition of the British slave trade enforced?

options.text: By voluntary compliance from British merchants only

The Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron (formed 1808, based at Sierra Leone) intercepted slave ships off the African coast; by the 1860s it had captured around 1,600 ships and freed around 150,000 enslaved Africans
By signing treaties with no enforcement mechanism
By immediately ending all transatlantic shipping

items.reveal:
The West Africa Squadron began with two ships and grew to around 25 by mid-century — about a sixth of the Royal Navy. Captures were brought before Vice-Admiralty courts at Freetown; freed Africans were resettled in Sierra Leone or recruited as 'Liberated African' sailors.

The squadron's mortality rate was very high — yellow fever, malaria, and combat. By the 1840s, treaties with Portugal, Spain and others widened the squadron's powers.

The US South continued importing enslaved people illegally until the Civil War, but the Atlantic trade was largely suppressed by the 1860s. Brazil — the last major importer — banned the trade in 1850 and abolished slavery in 1888.
items.why: Abolishing a trade is different from enforcing the ban. Britain's commitment of naval power for over 60 years made 1807 effective — and reframed the slave trade as an international policing problem.

items.title: Henry VIII had six wives — divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived
items.claim: What is the standard rhyme for Henry VIII's wives' fates?

options.text: All six were executed

'Divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived' — Catherine of Aragon (annulled), Anne Boleyn (executed 1536), Jane Seymour (died after childbirth 1537), Anne of Cleves (annulled), Catherine Howard (executed 1542), Catherine Parr (survived him)
Henry had only two wives
All six died of plague

items.reveal_title: Six queens, three Catherines, two Annes
items.reveal:
Catherine of Aragon (m. 1509, annulled 1533, died 1536) was Henry's brother Arthur's widow. Anne Boleyn (m. 1533, executed 19 May 1536) bore Elizabeth I. Jane Seymour (m. 1536, died 24 October 1537) bore Edward VI.

Anne of Cleves (m. and annulled 1540) negotiated a comfortable settlement and lived until 1557. Catherine Howard (m. 1540, executed 13 February 1542) was perhaps 17 at marriage. Catherine Parr (m. 1543) outlived Henry (d. January 1547) and died in 1548.

The rhyme 'divorced, beheaded, died' is a 19th-century mnemonic; Tudor contemporaries did not summarise the marriages this way.
items.why: Royal personal lives can carry constitutional weight. Henry's marital sequence drove the English Reformation, the succession crisis, and ultimately the Tudor dynasty's extinction with Elizabeth I in 1603.

items.title: Augustus claimed to have 'restored the Republic' in 27 BCE
items.claim: How did Augustus describe his own constitutional position?

options.text: As king and emperor explicitly

He claimed to have 'restored the Republic' in his Res Gestae (the inscription set up at his mausoleum) — taking the title 'princeps' (first citizen) and refusing the title rex; in reality he held most magisterial powers and military command
As a Greek tyrant
As a temporary dictator only

items.reveal:
Octavian (Caesar's adopted heir) defeated Mark Antony at Actium in 31 BCE. In 27 BCE he made a show of restoring power to the Senate and was given the name Augustus ('revered'). He held tribunician power, imperium (military command) over the key provinces, and the title princeps senatus.

The Res Gestae Divi Augusti — 'The Achievements of the Divine Augustus' — was a long inscription set up at his death (14 CE) listing his deeds. It claims constitutional propriety throughout.

The Republic was, in effect, over. The Principate (early empire) lasted until the crises of the third century. The pretence of republican forms outlasted Augustus by centuries.
items.why: Political systems can hollow out while keeping their old names. Augustus's 'restored Republic' was already an autocracy in everything but name — a useful case in how institutional language can mask transformation.

items.title: Naseby (1645) was won by the New Model Army
items.claim: What was the Battle of Naseby?

options.text: An early Royalist victory in 1642

On 14 June 1645, Parliament's New Model Army under Sir Thomas Fairfax (with Oliver Cromwell commanding cavalry) decisively defeated Charles I's army in Northamptonshire — capturing his correspondence with foreign powers and ending hope of Royalist victory
A naval engagement in the English Channel
The first battle of the war (1642)

items.reveal:
The New Model Army had been formed by ordinance in February 1645 — the first national professional army, of around 22,000 men. Naseby was its first major test. Parliament's forces of around 14,000 defeated the king's 9,000.

The king's baggage train was captured, including his correspondence — letters showing he was negotiating with Irish Catholics and foreign Catholic powers for military aid. The 'King's Cabinet Opened' (published July 1645) destroyed remaining sympathy in Parliament.

Charles surrendered to the Scots in May 1646. He was handed to Parliament in 1647, tried for treason in January 1649, and executed on 30 January.
items.why: Single battles can decide wars. Naseby ended the Royalist field army; the king's captured letters ended any chance of negotiated settlement. The two together made the regicide of 1649 possible.

items.title: Clause 39 of Magna Carta is the ancestor of due process
items.claim: What does Clause 39 of Magna Carta (1215) say?

options.text: It establishes universal suffrage

'No free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions... except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land' — the basis of habeas corpus and due process traditions
It abolishes the monarchy
It guarantees free trade

items.reveal:
The 1215 charter had 63 clauses, mostly about specific feudal grievances. Clause 39 (combined with clause 40 — 'to no one will we sell, to no one deny or delay right or justice') is the source of the due process tradition.

'Free man' (liber homo) in 1215 was a small minority — perhaps a tenth of the population. The protection was extended over centuries by reissue, interpretation and common-law development.

The US Fifth Amendment (1791) — 'nor be deprived of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law' — directly echoes Magna Carta. The phrase 'due process of law' was first used in a 1354 reissue of the charter under Edward III.
items.why: Founding documents have specific clauses that travel further than others. Clause 39 of Magna Carta is the single most influential sentence in English-language constitutional law — its 21st-century echoes are direct.

items.title: Constantine legalised Christianity in 313 CE but converted slowly
items.claim: When did the Roman Empire become Christian?

options.text: Constantine made Christianity the state religion in 312

The Edict of Milan (313) granted religious toleration; Constantine increasingly favoured Christianity but was baptised only on his deathbed in 337; Theodosius I made Christianity the state religion by the Edict of Thessalonica in 380
Augustus was already Christian
The empire remained pagan until 600 CE

items.reveal:
Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge (28 October 312) over Maxentius came after a reported vision of the Chi-Rho symbol with 'in hoc signo vinces' (in this sign you will conquer). The Edict of Milan, agreed with Licinius in 313, granted religious toleration to all.

Constantine convened the Council of Nicaea (325) and built churches across the empire. He moved the capital to Constantinople (founded 330). He was baptised on his deathbed in 337 by an Arian bishop, Eusebius of Nicomedia.

The Edict of Thessalonica (380) under Theodosius I made Nicene Christianity the state religion. Pagan worship was progressively restricted; the Olympic Games were banned in 393.
items.why: Religious change at imperial scale is a process, not a moment. The 67 years between Milan and Thessalonica saw a tolerant empire become a Christian one — a transformation studied by every subsequent religious-political shift.

items.title: The First Crusade captured Jerusalem with massacre in 1099
items.claim: What happened when the First Crusade took Jerusalem?

options.text: Crusaders left peacefully after victory

On 15 July 1099 crusaders breached the walls; over the following days a massacre of Muslim and Jewish inhabitants followed — chroniclers (including Raymond of Aguilers) recorded slaughter so extensive that 'one waded in blood up to the ankles'
The city surrendered without combat
Jerusalem was bypassed for Cairo

items.reveal:
The crusade had left Europe in 1096. After taking Antioch (1098), the army of around 14,000 reached Jerusalem in June 1099. The walls were breached on 15 July; the massacre that followed killed thousands. Jewish inhabitants who took refuge in a synagogue were burned alive.

Godfrey of Bouillon was elected 'Defender of the Holy Sepulchre' (refusing the title of king); his brother Baldwin became Baldwin I of Jerusalem in 1100. The Kingdom of Jerusalem lasted until 1291 (fall of Acre).

Saladin recaptured Jerusalem in 1187 with notably less violence — he allowed inhabitants to ransom themselves and many to leave safely, in deliberate contrast to 1099.
items.why: Religious warfare in the high Middle Ages was often atrocious. The 1099 massacre shaped Muslim-Christian relations for centuries — and the comparison with Saladin's 1187 conduct is one that Muslim sources have made repeatedly.

items.title: Domesday Book was completed in around a year
items.claim: How quickly was Domesday Book compiled?

options.text: Over several decades
Commissioned by William I at Christmas 1085, the survey of around 13,000 places was largely completed within a year, with the final two-volume Great Domesday and Little Domesday produced by 1086
It took 100 years to complete
It was never finished

items.reveal:
Commissioners visited each shire, taking sworn testimony from jury panels of local landholders. The survey recorded who held land before and after 1066, the value, the population, the resources (ploughs, mills, fishponds, pasture).

The survey was unprecedented in medieval Europe in its speed and detail. The name 'Domesday' (judgment day) was applied by users by around 1100 — they could not appeal against its findings, as they could not appeal against the Last Judgment.

The manuscripts (Great Domesday for most of England, Little Domesday for Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex) survive at The National Archives in Kew.
items.why: Medieval government was capable of administrative effort that would not be matched in Europe for centuries. Domesday's speed and accuracy is one of the strongest counters to the 'Dark Ages' frame.

items.title: Elizabeth I's wardrobe was a political instrument
items.claim: How extensive was Elizabeth I's wardrobe at her death?

options.text: A modest collection of state robes

Inventories at her death (1603) recorded around 2,000 gowns, gifts and ceremonial robes; she owned around 80 wigs after smallpox scarring in 1562 and used ceruse make-up to maintain the 'Mask of Youth' image
She refused to wear ornament
She owned 50,000 dresses

items.reveal:
Elizabeth survived smallpox in October 1562 with scarring on her face and neck. Ceruse (white lead and vinegar) gave the white complexion seen in portraits — slowly toxic with long-term use.

Nicholas Hilliard's 'Treatise Concerning the Arte of Limning' (1598-1602) reports that painters were instructed not to show shadow on the queen's face after about 1590 — the 'Mask of Youth' image preserved her as eternally young.

The wardrobe was renewed by gifts from courtiers, who chose colours, materials and embroidered devices loaded with political meaning. Roy Strong's 'Gloriana' (1987) catalogued the visual programme.
items.why: Elizabethan court politics was conducted partly through clothes. The 'Virgin Queen' image was constructed by carefully managed wardrobe, portraiture and pageant — a sustained branding exercise of the monarchy.

items.title: British smallpox vaccination became compulsory in 1853
items.claim: When did vaccination become compulsory in the UK?

options.text: Immediately after Jenner's 1796 experiment

The Vaccination Act 1853 made infant smallpox vaccination compulsory in England and Wales; the 1867 Act introduced fines for non-compliance; the 1898 Act allowed a 'conscientious objection' exemption after mass protest
Compulsion was never introduced
It was made compulsory only in 1948

items.reveal:
Edward Jenner published his cowpox technique in 1798. The 1853 Vaccination Act required parents to vaccinate infants within three months of birth, or face fines. The 1867 Act added imprisonment for repeated refusal.

The Leicester Anti-Vaccination League (founded 1869) led mass protest; in 1885, around 100,000 marched in Leicester against the Act. The 'Leicester method' substituted isolation and sanitation for compulsory vaccination — and Leicester's smallpox mortality remained low.

The 1898 Act introduced 'conscientious objection' as a legal category. Smallpox was declared eradicated globally by WHO on 8 May 1980 — the only human disease ever eradicated.
items.why: Public health enforcement has always provoked opposition. The 19th-century vaccination debate created the legal category of 'conscientious objection' — a concept later used for military service and other state requirements.

items.title: The Soviet Union dissolved on 26 December 1991
items.claim: How did the USSR end?

options.text: By military defeat

After Gorbachev's perestroika and glasnost reforms, the August 1991 hardline coup failed, Baltic states declared independence, Yeltsin took power in Russia; the USSR was formally dissolved by the Belavezha Accords (8 December) and Gorbachev's resignation (25 December); the Supreme Soviet voted itself out of existence on 26 December 1991
Through Chinese intervention
By a vote of all citizens in 1989

items.reveal:
Mikhail Gorbachev became General Secretary in March 1985. Perestroika (restructuring) and glasnost (openness) loosened Soviet controls. Eastern European communism collapsed in 1989. The Baltic states declared independence in 1990-91.

The August 1991 coup by hardliners against Gorbachev failed within three days when Boris Yeltsin rallied resistance from a tank outside the Russian White House. Real power shifted from the USSR to Russia.

The Belavezha Accords (8 December 1991) saw the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus declare the USSR dissolved. The Alma-Ata Protocol (21 December) added eight more republics. Gorbachev resigned on 25 December; the Supreme Soviet voted on 26 December.
items.why: The largest peaceful end of a superpower in history. The mechanism — internal reform, failed counter-coup, voluntary dissolution by republics — has shaped how subsequent transitions have been imagined.

items.title: Trial by ordeal was banned by the Church in 1215
items.claim: When did European trial by ordeal end?

options.text: It remained the standard method until the 18th century
The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) forbade priests from participating, effectively ending the practice in most of Christian Europe — replaced by jury trial in England
It never existed in England
It was banned by Magna Carta

items.reveal:
Trial by ordeal — boiling water, hot iron, cold water — relied on priests blessing the test and reading the result (the wound's healing pattern after three days, whether the accused floated or sank). The Fourth Lateran Council under Innocent III forbade clergy participation in 1215.

In England, the result was the rise of jury trial. The petty jury (12 men deciding facts) gradually replaced ordeal through the 13th century. Trial by combat survived longer for some civil matters — formally abolished only in 1819.

Women accused of witchcraft were sometimes 'swum' (an unofficial ordeal) into the 18th century — but this was outside formal legal procedure.
items.why: Legal procedure is shaped by religious authority. The 1215 Lateran Council in Rome ended a centuries-old English legal practice — and helped create the jury system that became central to common-law tradition.

items.title: The Great Pyramid was the world's tallest building for 3,800 years
items.claim: How tall is the Great Pyramid and how long did it hold the height record?

options.text: Around 50 m, surpassed within centuries

Originally around 146.7 m (now around 138.5 m after loss of casing stones), built around 2560 BCE for Pharaoh Khufu — the tallest human structure until Lincoln Cathedral's spire (around 160 m) in 1311 CE
Around 500 m
It has been the world's tallest building continuously

items.reveal:
The Great Pyramid of Giza was built during the Fourth Dynasty for Khufu (Greek: Cheops). It contains around 2.3 million blocks averaging 2.5 tonnes each. The construction took perhaps 20 years using rotating labour gangs (around 20,000-30,000 workers at peak).

Lincoln Cathedral's central spire (completed around 1311) finally exceeded it. That spire collapsed in 1549. The Eiffel Tower (1889) finally and permanently dethroned the pyramid as the world's tallest human structure.

The original outer casing of polished white Tura limestone was largely removed in medieval Cairo for building material — including for the Hassan Mosque (1356).
items.why: Scale matters in human achievement. A building completed 4,500 years ago held the height record for 3,800 of those years — a testament to ancient engineering that modern construction took until the 19th century to surpass.
